events.title: China Isn’t Buying Silicon Valley’s Call for an AI Slowdown
events.summary: For years, many of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley have argued that the US is locked in an AI arms race with China and that the consequences of losing would be disastrous. But over the past week, those same executives have started emphasizing a different message. AI has the potential to become so dangerous , tech leaders say, that the two countries urgently need to work together to slow the race down. “Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in a blog post published Saturday titled “ We Must Pace the Frontier .” China’s government and AI companies have made it clear that they’re deeply skeptical of Amodei’s proposal, but not because they want to keep blindly racing ahead or don’t believe the technology poses serious risks. The problem the Chinese government and Chinese AI companies see is far simpler. They think they’re being offered a bad deal. “The AI safety community in China is growing and shares many of the same concerns that American labs do,” says Kevin Xu, founder of the technology hedge fund Interconnected Capital and a former White House staffer under President Barack Obama. “The gulf lies between an Anthropic-led vision that would only subjugate and restrict China first to maximize leverage before talking. Meanwhile, China would only talk if it’s being treated from a position of equals.” Amodei wrote that a “key part” of the slowdown strategy should be ensuring that the US and other democracies maintain “as large as possible” a lead in AI development over autocracies like China. To do that, he urged the US to take steps including cracking down on chip smuggling and preventing unauthorized model distillation by Chinese companies. “His essay specifically says the pacing of AI is conditional to increasing the lead over China," says Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis and a digital fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, “which makes the proposal feel inauthentic to Chinese readers.” Amodei went on to make what might seem like a heroic leap in logic: He argued that weakening China’s AI industry would somehow give the US more leverage and make “an agreement more likely in the future.” How, exactly, that is supposed to entice Beijing to come to the negotiating table is left unexplained. (To Amodei’s credit, he later admitted in a television interview that he has “no idea how to negotiate with China.”) The government officials, AI researchers, and other prominent commentators in China who responded to Amodei haven’t argued that AI poses no risks. But many of them clearly resent the idea that their country should simultaneously be treated as an essential governance partner and a competitor that needs to be constrained. When asked about Amodei’s blog post on Monday at a press conference, Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, didn’t mince words: He described the proposal as “fearmongering, confrontation, and vicious competition” that would only hamper global AI cooperation efforts. The next day, the ministry also stressed that “China puts equal emphasis on development and security in terms of AI.” The mixed comments are reflective of another reason that Beijing may be less receptive to the Anthropic CEO’s warnings than other audiences. Unlike many of the loudest voices in Silicon Valley, China’s leaders are not primarily concerned about so-called existential risks from AI, such as the possibility that a rogue agent could kill everyone on Earth. Like in many other policy areas, Beijing’s prevailing anxiety is that AI could disrupt domestic social stability or threaten the Chinese Communist Party’s grip on power. “Beijing finds it difficult to take these calls at face value partly because it’s skeptical of the possibility of achieving AGI and doubtful of the narrative that AI poses extreme risks to humanity,” says Michelle Nie, a visiting fellow at the Center for a New American Security focused on national security and artificial intelligence. “Although Beijing is starting to recognize loss-of-control risks, the risk that Beijing seems most worried about is the threat AI could pose to CCP rule.” In a recent essay , China’s minister of state security Chen Yixin warned that AI could fuel political disinformation, cyberattacks, espionage, social unrest, and new military threats. He spent far less time on the kinds of doomsday scenarios that frequently preoccupy people at US frontier AI labs. “Chinese policymakers tend to read US companies’ calls for AI safety as instrumental,” says Nie. “They believe that US companies are seeking to inflate their own value ahead of potential IPOs or to slow down their competitors, which are primarily Chinese companies at this point.

events.title: Trump escalates war on federal data
events.summary: The nerdy, traditionally apolitical world of federal data is increasingly getting swept up in the Trump administration's push to control every level of government. Across the federal government, agencies are changing how they collect and publicize information. More and more, politics and ideology are part of the equation. Why it matters: Reliable, unbiased data informs nearly everything the federal government does — from distributing benefits and enforcing workplace discrimination laws to responding to public health threats. Driving the news: The administration's moves in recent weeks span an array of agencies and types of data. 🩺 Measles. Reuters reported that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked the CDC director to remove a reference to two deaths in Pennsylvania from its online tally of measles cases. The move came after the CDC had already accepted Pennsylvania officials' explanation that the deaths were linked to measles. Kennedy and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro had spent days sparring on social media, each accusing the other of politicizing the deaths. Kennedy is a longtime vaccine skeptic. 🏡 Census Bureau. Last month, the Commerce Department did away with language barring political interference that had been part of the department's scientific integrity policy , NPR reported . The department oversees the Census Bureau and several other agencies. The move came after the bureau issued an unauthored report — promptly touted by President Trump — that found that 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election. The team behind the report, however, included officials with ties to the Trump-linked America First Institute . ⚠️ Anti-discrimination. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission is planning to stop collecting data that's helped the agency investigate claims of workplace discrimination, The Guardian reported . For 60 years, the agency has examined the demographic makeup of company workforces to enforce anti-discrimination laws. The EEOC is now planning to do away with the so-called EEO-1 reports, which require companies to provide data on their workforces broken down by race, ethnicity, sex and job title. The move comes amid a broader Trump administration crackdown on DEI — diversity, equity and inclusion — initiatives. At a July hearing, Andrea Lucas, an EEOC commissioner appointed by Trump, said the data collection was burdensome for employers and encouraged discrimination against white workers, per the Guardian. What they're saying: "The level of politicization in this administration is beyond anything I've seen," says Denice Ross, former U.S. chief data scientist and currently director of the Data Policy Institute at the Federation of American Scientists. "I've been doing this work for 25 years." Zoom out: Fears about the handling of data that doesn't comport with Trump's worldview have been around for years . Last year, Trump fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics hours after the agency released disappointing jobs numbers. "Today's Jobs Numbers were RIGGED in order to make the Republicans, and ME, look bad," Trump wrote. The Department of Homeland Security has stopped regularly publishing comprehensive immigration enforcement statistics, including data that allowed outsiders to assess the administration's deportation efforts. The official who oversaw DHS's independent statistics office resigned in July, The Atlantic reported . According to a tracker run by former federal government data scientists, 38 datasets have been eliminated since Trump returned to office. Hundreds of other datasets have been altered or disrupted. The other side: "The Trump administration is committed to providing the American people with timely, accurate, and relevant data that's helpful to inform meaningful research, discourse, and decision-making," White House spokesman Kush Desai said. "Ensuring public health and other critical data actually reflect reality while refusing to waste taxpayer resources on ideological pet projects are all important parts of that mission." The bottom line: "We really take data for granted," Ross said. "It's invisible infrastructure, like a bridge or cell service. We don't notice until it's gone."

events.title: BT Email users hit by barrage of unsolicited password reset PINs
events.summary: UPDATED BT Email customers say they have been bombarded with hundreds – and in one case more than 1,000 – unsolicited password reset messages, leaving the telco investigating what is causing the deluge. The reports began appearing on BT's community forums over the weekend, with customers describing sudden bursts of PIN messages arriving within minutes despite them making no attempt to reset their passwords. One customer said they received between 50 and 70 PIN texts "in the space [of] a few minutes," while a second reported more than 100. A third said the number had passed 500, and another claimed to have received more than 1,000. One BT customer who contacted The Register separately said they had received around 300 password reset emails over the previous 24 hours, typically arriving in bursts of around 50 within a minute before stopping for several hours. BT has acknowledged the problem but has yet to explain what is behind it. "We are aware that some customers have received a large number of password reset pin messages and we are actively investigating the cause of this," a BT moderator said on the company's community forum. "If you have received multiple messages like this, please ignore them and remain vigilant for any unusual activity with further messages or unexpected calls." BT added that customers' email accounts are secure and that those receiving the messages do not need to take any action. At least one customer, however, claims someone accessed their account during the PIN barrage. The user said they lost access to both their email and BT ID overnight, but managed to request a PIN before whoever was accessing the account could change the telephone number attached to it. That account has not been independently verified, and it isn't clear whether the apparent takeover was connected to the flood of PIN messages. The cause of the wider problem remains a mystery. It isn’t yet clear whether it’s the result of someone deliberately hammering a password recovery mechanism, a fault within BT's systems, or something else entirely. The Register has asked BT how many customers are affected, whether the messages are being generated by external password-reset attempts, and whether it has found any evidence of malicious activity. We've also asked the telco what rate limiting it applies to password reset requests, given reports of hundreds of PINs arriving within minutes, and whether both email and SMS messages are affected. BT says it's investigating. In the meantime, some customers are getting enough PINs to start their own lottery. ® Updated at 09.49 UTC on September 17, 2026 to add: "We are aware that a small number of customers have received repeated password reset PIN messages via text or email. We have implemented a number of mitigations to prevent further password reset messages from being sent, and we’re contacting any impacted customers to advise them to ignore the PIN messages they have received. Customers do not need to take any further action, and we continue to monitor the issue."

events.title: The public wants a say in AI development
events.summary: Democratic and Republican voters agree that the American public should decide the future of AI development, not billionaires in Silicon Valley, according to new polling shared first with Semafor. The poll was commissioned for a new organization launched by Alex Bores , who made a name for himself as a top target of the AI industry in his failed bid for Congress in New York. Though AI ranked last on a list of 13 issues that 1,502 registered voters polled this month said they care about, half said AI is moving too fast and 86% identified lack of regulation as a problem. Only 18% of those polled think the US falling behind China competitively is a problem, a risk President Donald Trump has cited in opposing regulation. While just 36% polled said they had heard about incidents like the Hugging Face hack, “support for reasonable regulations is actually quite correlated with all these other issues,” Bores told Semafor Tuesday in Washington on the sidelines of the “pro-human” summit attended by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Steve Bannon. The poll’s results, Bores argued, show that “if you show good work on AI, you’re winning over voters, even though AI isn’t their top issue.” Bores’ new organization, Who Decides, aims to help the broader Democratic coalition unite around a “shared baseline” for AI protections. The organization will help traditionally Democratic groups like labor and civil society craft AI policy messages, Bores said. “As a Democrat, I say this with love, but we turn everything into a circular firing squad, and I think it’s really, really important that on this issue, where we have powerful, well-resourced enemies that don’t want there to be any regulation whatsoever, that we are all on the same tea,” he said.

events.title: Household income hits record, but lower earners lose ground
events.summary: Data: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, 1968 to 2026 Annual Social and Economic Supplements ; Note: Census identifies breaks in the series in 2013 and 2017 due to methodological changes; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios U.S. household income hit a record in 2025, but the lowest earners barely shared in the gains, new Census data show. Why it matters: On paper, Americans look richer than ever. But broader measures of financial security show millions still getting squeezed by medical costs , uneven income gains and a thinning public safety net. The 2025 Census report largely captures the economy before the major safety-net reductions in President Trump's " Big Beautiful Bill" took hold. That makes this year's record income and near-record-low official poverty numbers an important benchmark for measuring what happens next. By the numbers: Real median household income rose 2.6% to $87,460 in 2025, the highest inflation-adjusted level since Census records began in 1967. Median post-tax household income climbed 3.1% to $76,060. The official poverty rate fell for a third straight year, dropping slightly to 10.2%, or about 34.5 million people. Child poverty fell to a record-low 13.4%, while poverty among Hispanics dropped to an unprecedented 13.9%. State of play: The economy delivered historic topline numbers without spreading the gains evenly. Income among the wealthiest 10% of Americans rose 1.7%, while income among the bottom 10% showed no significant change — indicating that the low-income households largely missed out on the gains. Households at the 90th percentile earned about $261,300, more than 13 times the roughly $20,010 earned at the 10th percentile. The top fifth of households captured 52.4% of all household income. The bottom fifth reported earning just 3%. Zoom in: Latinos offer one of the clearest examples of the split-screen economy in 2025. Hispanic poverty fell to its lowest level since Census began tracking it in 1973. But the median household income among Hispanics, $73,260, showed no significant change from 2024. Meanwhile, 21.8% of Hispanic adults ages 19 to 64 were uninsured in 2025, down a bit from the previous year — but still the highest uninsured rate among the major racial and ethnic groups shown by Census Yes, but: Big racial income gaps remain even as some groups posted gains. Asian American households had the highest median income at $126,300 in 2025, compared with $91,930 for white households and $59,980 for Black American households. Black Americans' household income rose 4.8% from 2024 and whites' household income rose 3%, while Asian Americans' household income showed no significant change. Zoom out: A broader measure of hardship paints a less rosy picture. The Supplemental Poverty Measure , which factors in taxes, government benefits, housing, work and medical expenses, held statistically steady at 13.1% — nearly 3 percentage points above the government's official poverty rate. Medical expenses put an estimated 7.7 million more people below the supplemental poverty line in 2025, the Census Bureau said. Between the lines: Health insurance coverage held steady overall in 2025. The uninsured rate remained statistically unchanged at 7.9%, or 26.7 million people. Medicaid coverage fell 0.5 percentage points nationally, from 17.6% to 17.1% of the population — representing about 1.4 million fewer people with Medicaid coverage in 2025 than in the previous year Among adults ages 19 to 64, 17.3% had public health coverage — including Medicaid, Medicare and VA/CHAMPVA coverage — down 0.5 percentage points from 2024. Census says the decline was driven by a 0.6-point drop in Medicaid coverage among working-age adults. What we're watching: The 2025 numbers may represent the last snapshot before major federal safety-net cuts begin showing up in the Census data, Robert Greenstein, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution, tells Axios.

events.title: Tech giants launch flexible-power coalition for data centers
events.summary: A new coalition launched Wednesday is seeking a triple win for a data center industry that lately has struggled to notch any wins at all. The big picture: Tech giants Google and Nvidia are partnering with startup Emerald AI to back data centers that can flex their power demand — a strategy they say could curb electricity prices, mollify angry neighbors and grow the economy with more AI infrastructure. The launch comes amid mounting backlash to data centers centered on their resource impacts and power prices, and new polling shows the public-opinion challenge is getting steeper. What they're saying: "It's really a win-win-win solution," said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at Nvidia, in a call with reporters Monday ahead of the official launch of the coalition, called the AI Energy Management Alliance . State of play: The coalition brings together 20 companies and organizations spanning the AI and energy sectors, including Anthropic, utilities National Grid and AES, and power producers Constellation, NRG and RWE. The group is technically a relaunch. An earlier iteration, the Advanced Energy Management Alliance, was founded in 2014 to advocate for demand-response companies but had become largely inactive, Emerald AI CEO Varun Sivaram said on Monday's call. The revamped group is narrowly focused on making AI data centers more flexible power users — and convincing regulators and utilities to reward them for it. Friction point: A whopping 84% of Americans say they're concerned about data centers' impact on local electricity prices, according to new AP-NORC/University of Chicago Energy Policy Institute polling released Wednesday . More than half of Americans are extremely or very concerned about AI's environmental impacts, up from 41% a year ago. In a rare point of bipartisan agreement, roughly equal shares of Democrats and Republicans — 79% and 76%, respectively — support requiring data center developers to pay for the grid upgrades needed to support them. How it works: Data centers have traditionally been treated as giant, round-the-clock power users. The coalition wants to change the rules so facilities that can reliably cut their grid demand when electricity supplies are tight can get connected faster and potentially avoid some costly grid upgrades. The flexibility could come from shifting or pausing AI computing jobs, tapping batteries or nearby power generation, coalition leaders said. Google has committed 1 gigawatt of power demand it can reduce when needed through utility agreements nationwide, said Tyler Norris, Google's head of advanced energy market innovation. The group plans to push the approach with federal and state regulators, regional grid operators and utilities. Yes, but: The bargain depends on data centers actually delivering the flexibility they promise. Sivaram said facilities should qualify for faster or larger connections only if their ability to cut demand is "verifiable and enforceable." Reality check: Convincing communities that this complicated solution can actually address their concerns will be a tall order. "Power-flexible data centers are a wonky topic," Sivaram told Axios. His pitch: Data centers could cut their electricity use when the grid is stressed, helping avoid costly infrastructure while bringing in revenue that can support other electricity users. The goal, Sivaram said, is to turn data centers into "good grid citizens" that communities see as assets rather than burdens. What we're watching: Whether regulators actually create the fast lane the coalition wants. Federal regulators in June directed regional grid operators to examine new options for connecting large, flexible power users, providing an opening for the approach AEMA is advocating. Editor's note: Amy Harder is a fellow at the University of Chicago's Institute for Climate and Sustainable Growth, but was not involved in the polling and received no advance access beyond that provided to other journalists. Editor's note: This story has been corrected to note that 76% of Republicans (not 78%) support requiring data center developers to pay for grid upgrades.

events.title: Arizona Lowered the Bar for Its English Fluency Test. Experts Say It Will Harm Students in the Long Run.
events.summary: Samantha Ramos teaches students in her English language development class at John B. Wright Elementary School in Tucson, Arizona. Cassidy Araiza for ProPublica Samantha Ramos stood at the front of her second grade classroom, a small mic clipped to her lanyard amplifying her instructions as she began a phonics lesson. “Can we get our arms ready?” asked Ramos, who’s taught at the John B. Wright Elementary School in Tucson, Arizona, for 15 years. She brought her right palm to her left shoulder as the students imitated her movements. Ramos, who specializes in teaching English as a second language, was leading a lesson that day on the short “i” sound. She told the students to pronounce each letter with a different gesture — touching the shoulder for the “w,” the elbow for the “i” and the hand for the double “l” — before sounding out the word “will.” They repeated the process for other short “i” words — “dig,” “wig” and “fit.” The lesson is part of a daily block of language instruction, ranging from two to four hours long, that Arizona students learning English as a second language are required to take. The students, most of them Spanish-speaking Latino children, remain in the program, separated for part of that time from their peers whose primary language is English, until they pass a test showing they’re fluent enough to learn in a mainstream classroom. The program is known as “structured English immersion,” or colloquially as “English-only” because all instruction is required to be in English. This limits their time for core subjects, like math and science, that are critical to academic success and college readiness. Arizona is the only state with English-only laws still in effect for its public schools. But the number of students enrolled in the curriculum has tumbled dramatically this year. At the Tucson Unified School District, where Ramos teaches, the percentage of test-taking students who scored high enough to be classified as proficient in English more than doubled — from 10% in 2025 to 24% in 2026. Rather than a big leap in fluency, however, the test results reflect the Arizona Department of Education lowering the grade needed to pass. The changes were approved by outgoing Superintendent of Public Instruction Tom Horne, a longtime Republican defender of Arizona’s English-only policies. Experts warn this change will do lasting harm to tens of thousands of Arizona students who will exit the structured English immersion program before they know the language well enough to succeed. Such students are already part of the lowest-performing group on standardized tests, and the loss of specialized instruction could further harm their long-term academic success, according to education researchers. Past attempts by the Arizona Department of Education to reclassify large numbers of children learning English as fluent prompted federal investigations by the departments of Justice and Education. Federal officials contended placing such students in classrooms where they struggled because they lacked knowledge of English violated their civil and educational rights, and Arizona agreed to a settlement more than a decade ago. What’s happening now could be a repeat of that, said Katie Bernstein, an applied linguist and professor of early childhood education at Arizona State University. “If you’re put in a class where you don’t understand what’s going on at all, you’re not learning language or content,” she said. “And so those are the worst outcomes of all, are students who are not given any language services.” Ramos teaches her students phonics during a daily block of English-language immersion. Cassidy Araiza for ProPublica Nearly 1 in 10 students enrolled in Arizona public and charter schools marked in their school registration forms they speak a language other than English at home. State law mandates that they be assessed for fluency and placed in structured English immersion, and each spring they take the Arizona English Language Learner Assessment, or AZELLA, to measure their progress in reading, writing, speaking and listening. This approach has been required since Arizona voters passed a 2000 ballot initiative, Proposition 203, banning bilingual education in public schools. Still, officials have periodically made changes to the proficiency test. The U.S. departments of Justice and Education determined the version of AZELLA administered between 2006 and 2012 — coinciding with Horne’s first two terms as the state’s top education official — was “not a valid measure of English language proficiency and readiness.” As a result, the state had removed at least 28,000 students from structured English immersion who still lacked proficiency in reading and writing the language. The Arizona Department of Education was found to be in violation of civil rights laws that ban discrimination on the basis of race and national origin by schools that receive federal funds. The state voluntarily entered a settlement , which stressed that the law requires “education agencies to take appropriate action to overcome language barriers that impede students’ equal participation in instructional programs.” Do You Have Experience With Arizona’s Structured English Immersion System, Also Called English-Only? Have stories to tell about how Arizona treats children learning English in public schools? Share your tips with Rafael Carranza at englishlearners@azluminaria.org . The settlement agreement stipulated that the state would immediately help school districts find the students who had been harmed and offer “reading and writing intervention services.” In the long term, the state was required to revamp the AZELLA test. Similar issues prompted a second voluntary settlement four years later , which instructed the state to raise the threshold for a test score to qualify as proficient in English. The state was also required to retest English-language learners using more rigorous standards, among other things. Ida Rose Florez, a psychologist and former professor and researcher at Arizona State University, conducted a study published in 2012 that found the AZELLA test was “ineffective and obsolete” and its results could be arbitrary. The research concluded there was no evidence the test could “accurately differentiate” between children who need English-language services and those who don’t. “What I examined, and what I saw, was a test that was absolutely not developed correctly,” Florez told Arizona Luminaria and ProPublica. “I don’t see any basis for validity whatsoever.” After dropping during the pandemic, AZELLA passing rates held steady at 12% statewide for three school years, including in 2025, when more than 118,000 took the test and just over 14,000 scored well enough to be reclassified as proficient. events.title: Justice threatens GOP showdown in West Virginia
events.summary: The News Jim Justice is getting the itch. And it could set up a battle of GOP titans. The West Virginia GOP senator is considering a run for his old job as governor in 2028, which would potentially set up a race between him and incumbent Gov. Patrick Morrisey. Justice told Semafor he’s “sure thinking about it” before quickly interjecting that he loves “what I’m doing here” in the Senate. He also jabbed at Morrisey but insisted he wants the governor to be successful: “Gov. Morrisey has a more difficult time bonding with people and everything, but beyond that, I want him to do great, I really do. I’m not in a food fight at all.” “I do love the people of West Virginia, and I spent eight years trying to build it back. Got it really going,” Justice continued. “I just want goodness for West Virginia, but I want goodness for the whole nation too. We’ll make a decision.” Know More West Virginia is a small state that’s also the home of bare-knuckled politics and big personalities. Republicans recruited Justice, a former Democrat, to run against former Sen. Joe Manchin, I-W.Va., in 2024, though Manchin ultimately decided against seeking reelection. Manchin narrowly defeated Morrisey in 2018, but Morrisey mounted a political comeback in 2024 by emerging from a crowded GOP primary and winning the governor’s mansion. A Morrisey ally told Semafor that Justice has myriad vulnerabilities and hasn’t had to win a tough GOP primary against someone like the incumbent governor (though Justice did easily defeat former Rep. Alex Mooney, R-W.Va., in 2024). The ally added that the conservative Club for Growth is already committed to opposing Justice, put Morrisey’s war chest at nearly $5 million across several political entities, and noted that Justice is in debt and is now sharing control of his family’s Greenbrier resort. But Justice said people in West Virginia are encouraging him to run: “You’re going to hear people come to you and say, ‘Boy, we’d love to have you back as governor.’ You know, that’s natural and everything. I don’t pay a whole lot of attention.” Manchin also flirted repeatedly with running for his old job as governor, which he used to call the “best job in the world.” Manchin never ran after serving in the Senate, but Senate Republicans believe Justice is more likely to run than not, according to several GOP sources. Regarding the 2028 governor race, Manchin said on Tuesday: “Can’t we get through this election before worrying about the next election?”

events.title: A new crop of Democratic early-state kingmakers rises for 2028
events.summary: The News One Democratic lawmaker — Rep. Jim Clyburn — played a pivotal role in the party’s 2020 presidential primary. Which means you’re about to hear a lot more from Reps. Teresa Leger Fernández, Steven Horsford, and Maggie Goodlander. Not to mention Sens. Ben Ray Luján, Jacky Rosen, Maggie Hassan, and more. Democrats’ decision to bump up New Mexico to their fourth primary spot in 2028, right after the now-familiar trio of South Carolina, Nevada, and New Hampshire, bestows growing prominence and sway on congressional delegations from all four states. Populous Michigan and Virginia, fifth and sixth on the primary calendar, will be right behind them. Democrats in the previous cast of early states are going to find new opportunities to wield their clout with a field that could easily number in the dozens. And lawmakers from states newer to the early-primary lineup are already preparing to elevate what matters to their constituents, as they get wooed by presidential aspirants. “I want them to come to New Mexico and look at the issues that we face,” said Fernández, D-N.M. “I want to see the candidates inspire the kind of communities that will make a difference in both the primary election and the general election.” With competitive midterm races happening in nearly all of the early states, potential Democratic presidential candidates are already on the trail with purple-district incumbents and candidates. Other lawmakers from early-primary states are fielding calls from 2028 contenders looking to appear with them. To name just a recent few: California Gov. Gavin Newsom appeared at the opening of a state party campaign office with Horsford; Maryland Gov. Wes Moore has done events for Nevada’s Democratic gubernatorial nominee, Aaron Ford; and New Mexico candidates have seen visits by former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker. “I’m not taking sides early. They’re all going to have to earn it,” said Horsford, whose district includes Las Vegas. He said he was hoping candidates would “understand that working-class people care about their healthcare, housing, childcare, elder care.” Rep. Gabe Vasquez, who represents a Trump-won New Mexico district, said Buttigieg had recently appeared with him. He named housing, water, and immigration as the top issues for candidates “to really come and understand how tough this economy truly is and what it’s going to take to fix it.” Democrats are also pouring into competitive Senate races in states like New Hampshire, where Rep. Chris Pappas is facing former Sen. John Sununu. But Luján says his colleagues are eager to visit him in New Mexico, too, even though Republicans struggled to even field a candidate against him. “Come on down and visit New Mexico, get to know the state. Get to know the people,” Luján told Semafor. “I certainly hope that whoever the next president of the United States is a Democrat and is a Democrat that understands New Mexico.” Luján’s fellow New Mexico senator, Martin Heinrich, said Democrats are still working through how they will host candidates in early-primary states in 2027 and 2028. But he said the new calendar is a big deal for New Mexico, which dropped off the swing-state map in 2008 after then-Sen. Barack Obama turned it blue. “We have a lot of really unique issues that are not something that you learn about through osmosis in other parts of the country,” Heinrich said. New Mexico will get “presidential candidates to care about water, public lands, national laboratories,” he added — “things that many of them just don’t have that much familiarity with.” Luján also said his state has great food, but cautioned candidates about a regional tripwire: feeling compelled to choose between the state’s famous green and red chiles. “It depends what they’re eating. Anyone that gives you an answer? They don’t know the state,” he said. “You can’t pick one.” Know More Democratic incumbents in tight races are hoping to reap electoral benefits from 2028 candidates who are coming through their districts. The visits tend to energize the base ahead of the midterms and may also broaden congressional candidates’ appeal. “I always look at the quality of events. Are they putting me in front of voters who I really haven’t connected with before? That’s sort of my No. 1 goal,” said Rep. Susie Lee, D-Nev., who represents a purple district. She called herself a “Buttigieg fan” this time and said she would endorse in the 2028 cycle, though she was waiting to learn more about other candidates’ positions. It helps that three early-primary states for 2028 are also hosting competitive Senate races this fall. Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., just campaigned in New Hampshire, and he’ll be heading to both Michigan and South Carolina, completing the trifecta. “We’ve never had a problem with getting people to pay attention to our state because we’ve always been a swing state. And I think the calendar probably heightens it,” said Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich. “We’re a good microcosm and often canary-in-the-coal-mine on issues, so we want to be in the mix.” Room for Disagreement Not every Democrat is sold on the new calendar. Those in New Hampshire say their state law supersedes the party’s revised order, which puts South Carolina ahead of them. “I continue to remind folks that New Hampshire has a state law, so we’re going to have the first primary,” Hassan told Semafor. “We are seeing a lot of people come up and campaign and support our candidates, and we continue to think that it’s really good for candidates, especially Democratic candidates, to be on the ground doing retail politics.” Nicholas and Burgess’ View The next generation of Democrats is clearly relishing the opportunity to help their party turn the page. After generations of candidates aligned their strategies around the Iowa caucuses and the first-in-the-nation primary in New Hampshire, Democratic candidates will now have to appeal to more diverse voters and work harder to stand out from a likely crowded field. But the huge slate of candidates could also prevent a repeat of Clyburn’s success in resuscitating Joe Biden’s campaign in 2020. The senior House Democrat became a kingmaker for Biden by giving him momentum heading into Super Tuesday after Biden’s poor showing in the first three states. This time, a half-dozen states are going before Super Tuesday and some of them have tons of delegates. That means Democratic contenders have a lot more lawmakers to woo. Notable Newsom said he wouldn’t run for president if former Vice President Kamala Harris did, CNN reported .

events.title: Congress’ AI safety window is closing
events.summary: The window for Congress to act on AI before the midterms is essentially shut — but a few senators are trying. Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., plans on Wednesday to seek unanimous consent for his bill to require an AI “kill switch” controlled by companies, not the government. Kennedy told Semafor he’s unsure whether anyone will object, but that his idea seems like the only doable one in the near term: An AI bill “would be impossible,” he said — “certainly, before the midterms; likely, during the lame duck.” Meanwhile, Sens. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., are pushing for a floor vote for their AI safety measure. And OpenAI chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane is pitching a three-pronged regulatory approach: industry safety practices, new legislation, and international leadership on safeguards by the Trump administration. He agreed that nothing is likely to happen before Election Day.

events.title: Girls flag football is fastest-growing high school sport
events.summary: Data: NFHS ; Map: Brad Jennings/Axios Girls flag football has become the fastest-growing high school sport, as tens of thousands take up a game that barely had a varsity footprint a few years ago. Why it matters: Few girls high school sports have moved from niche to mainstream so quickly, broadening athletic opportunities in the process. By the numbers: More than 102,000 girls played high school flag football in 2025-26, a 551% increase in the past four years, according to the National Federation of State High School Associations . Catch up quick: In 2024, just 12 states sanctioned high school girls flag football, viewed as a safer, more accessible version of America's most popular spectator sport. Today, 23 states plus Washington, D.C., sanction it as an official varsity sport , and 3,990 schools reported participants in 2025-26. The NFL is backing its growth, too. It has invested millions to launch and expand high school programs , and featured the sport in its Super Bowl commercials . Beyond high schools, flag football will debut at the 2028 Olympics, and at least 40 NCAA schools already offer it as a collegiate varsity sport. Reality check: It's not yet clear whether flag football is mostly creating new high school athletes or pulling girls from established sports. A recent Newsday analysis on Long Island found flag participation rising sharply while girls lacrosse, softball and track participation fell. What we're watching: Girls varsity wrestling is undergoing its own boom. All 50 states now report girls wrestling participation, and 40 state athletic associations hold girls wrestling championships, up from just five about a decade ago.

events.title: UK funds flying broadband stations with power beamed from below
events.summary: The UK's Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA) is funding projects aimed at delivering connectivity using high-flying aircraft, including technology to beam power from the ground to keep them in the air. Britain's science and technology body, inspired by America's DARPA but on a more modest budget, says it is backing 18 projects to develop aircraft capable of operating reliably and cost-effectively in the stratosphere, as part of a program known as Enduring Atmospheric Platforms. Success will be measured by whether any aircraft can continuously supply 300 W of power to a communications payload for an entire week, while holding station above the UK. The intent is to create an alternative to orbital satellites for providing connectivity to underserved parts of the UK and elsewhere in the world. These are known as high-altitude pseudo-satellites (HAPS). The agency says that satellites have been the default way to reach users or communities that are not well served by terrestrial networks, but their distance and orbits impose physical limits on what they can deliver. ARIA is allocating £70 million ($94 million) in funding over three and a half years for the projects, which will tackle the power and reliability challenges of sustained operations above the UK. The projects are split into three technical areas, with TA1 set to cover enabling technologies, TA2 comprising system integration and testing, and TA3 focused on deployment and communications. ARIA highlighted a project called Carousel from aerospace startup Menapia. This plans to produce a constellation of high-altitude multi-rotor aircraft, capable of routine operations at altitudes up to 20 km (12 miles), with the intention of forming a persistent "canopy" over the UK. Another is Enduring Drone Networks, being developed by VFP Aerospace, which is aiming for persistent presence via a relay team of units that will cycle between their service altitude and ground stations for recharging. It says it is targeting a production cost of £50,000 ($67,000) per drone. In the enabling technologies category, a firm called Hypanode Ltd is working on a fuel cell power system to deliver 20 times more energy than current battery technology. Scalable Laser Ltd is developing laser-based power beaming technology, pairing high-power laser diodes with advanced photovoltaic receivers, while Space Solar Engineering Ltd is looking at radio frequency power beaming to deliver continuous power to a HAPS aircraft. A more exotic-sounding technology is Stratospheric Navigation and Gravity (STRAT-NAV) from the University of Bath. This seeks to extend the endurance of HAPS craft by allowing them to predict and make use of atmospheric gravity waves – caused when air is forced upward by weather fronts or hills, and gravity pulls it back down, creating a ripple. "This research expands the UK's leadership in high-altitude platforms to become the place where this industry is designed, built, and scaled," says Rico Chandra, ARIA's program director for Enduring Atmospheric Platforms. "Getting there means backing bold ideas, from fixed-wing solar aircraft to designs nobody predicted, including aircraft that fly on spinning wings instead of propellers." ARIA funds teams of scientists and engineers to pursue cutting-edge research. It is a non-departmental public body sponsored by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST). It was until recently chaired by entrepreneur Matt Clifford, who stepped down after taking up a role with US AI firm Anthropic. The agency was also controversially spared being asked to make savings leading up to the UK government's Spending Review last year. ®

events.title: Bring on the AI swarms. They’re the only thing that can defend us now that AI is free
events.summary: Unpredictable token bills haunted the first half of 2026 as AI experimenters pushed deeper into the tech and often found useful results could only be achieved after surprising and unwelcome expenditure. We've gone from tokenmaxxers to tokenmisers, counting every character we send to AI services. That changed the way we used AI, focusing users on the ticking meter and unable to cast their eyes up and explore the possible. Those blinkers fell away in the middle of August when Alibaba delivered Qwen3.8-27B, byte-for-byte probably the most powerful language model ever created – and also capable of running on a high-spec laptop. The community of “local AI” enthusiasts noticed and have spent the intervening weeks whittling Qwen down to fit on an ever-widening array of devices, including – surprisingly – my M4 MacBook Air. Their work means millions of similar devices can now access near-frontier-level artificial intelligence from free software. The gap between my MacBook Air and a smartphone isn’t vast. As local AI developers continue whittling Qwen down to size, a few hundred million smartphones will also be capable of running top-tier AI. While that hasn't happened yet, it won't be more than six months away. At the rate things are unfolding, probably closer to six weeks. Suddenly, "good enough" AI isn't something that we will have to rent. We can have it, at no cost, on our desktops, our kitchen tables, our classrooms and in our pockets. That’s great, but also scary because we've been caught unprepared by AI effectively becoming free. Nobody yet knows what we will do with free AI, or if we are ready for it. On the positive side of the ledger, we stand to benefit from a growing “cognition surplus” that brings more thinking capacity into the home or office. Need to wrangle your way through a baroque accounting system? Give it to the AI. Sorting through twenty years of smartphone snaps? Again, let the AI do the heavy lifting. How about a personal newspaper gathered while you sleep, and presented on your tablet at the breakfast table? It's all doable now. All of that feels very much like something I remember clearly from the early 1980s, when the promise of the “home computer” was managing recipes. We knew the device would find a use, but it wasn't until the one-two punch of GUIs and the Web that most people had any real use for a home computer. That's exactly how this moment feels. Sure, managing smartphone photos will be helpful for millions, but the biggest win will be on the darker side of the ledger – where every bad actor – from script kiddies with a grudge through to the worst of the worst – now have equal access to powerful AI that will go with them everywhere. They’ll use it to lie, cheat and vex, at a speed and on a scale never before seen. To deal with that, we'll fight fire with fire. The most important job our AIs will be tasked with will be keeping us as safe as possible from other AIs. We’ll only be aware of this when it fails. But “good enough” AI and “intelligence everywhere” will enable resource pools and defensive techniques that our adversaries could never harness for themselves, so we stand a solid chance. ®

events.title: University of Manchester Uses NVIDIA Earth-2 to Forecast Air Pollution Across the UK
events.summary: Air pollution is a serious public health risk, contributing to an estimated 30,000 deaths in the U.K. alone last year. Data-driven insights can help — but computing air quality with traditional chemistry-based models is expensive, which limits how detailed they can be and how regularly they can be run. David Topping, a professor in the University of Manchester’s department of Earth and environmental science, saw that the NVIDIA Earth-2 family of open AI models and tools had cracked a related problem for weather forecasting — and asked whether the same generative frameworks could work for pollution fields. “The biggest challenge is the compute required to forecast air quality,” said Topping. “Once you put chemistry into weather models, they get really, really slow. So I said, why don’t we try using the generative frameworks that NVIDIA develops for climate and weather for pollution fields?” Working with the NVIDIA Earth-2 team, Topping and colleagues generated training data from existing chemistry-climate simulations, then trained Earth-2 CorrDiff — a generative downscaling model — on Isambard-AI, the U.K.’s national AI supercomputer in Bristol. The model worked on the first attempt. The team has since added Earth-2 StormCast, a model that enables time-dependent forecasts that directly use air quality observations, and showed the test-training and inference workflows running on the NVIDIA DGX Spark personal AI supercomputer. “To improve human health, it’s essential that we understand the impact of environmental stressors in the air we breathe,” said Topping. “Our U.K.-wide pollution model allows us to model potential future scenarios, such as predicting what would happen if different pollution-related government policy changes went into effect. Video credit: Bristol Centre for Supercomputing (BriCS) @ University of Bristol Another potential application is proactive air quality insights for healthcare organizations. Topping envisions a scenario where regional and national healthcare services could reach out to patients with conditions like asthma to let them know that air pollution is going to be high in their area tomorrow, or next week. The team is also exploring how the air pollution model could pair with data from edge AI devices to ingest real-time air quality data and drive real-time decision making, such as in the event of a wildfire. “The fact that this model trained in two days on Isambard-AI — and can now run on a DGX Spark sitting on a desk — changes who can do this science and how quickly,” said Niall Robinson, developer relations manager for weather and climate at NVIDIA. “We’re just at the beginning of what these open workflows can do globally.” “The ability to switch from one NVIDIA framework to another was really impressive,” said Hao Zhang, a doctoral student at the University of Manchester who trained StormCast on Isambard-AI. “We’re only just starting to explore how to use these frameworks in different ways to model complex pollution fields.” From National Supercomputer to the Desktop To retrain the Earth-2 model for air pollution, Topping and the team used a year’s worth of U.K. pollution data simulated at hourly intervals to generate a detailed, U.K.-wide pollution model at a resolution of 2-3 square kilometers. Running on a single, eight-GPU node on Isambard-AI — the U.K.’s most powerful AI supercomputer, packed with 5,448 NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchips delivering 21 exaflops of AI performance — the process took just two days. “Earth-2 CorrDiff has shown an incredibly efficient use of the world-class NVIDIA hardware inside Isambard-AI,” said Simon McIntosh-Smith, director of the Bristol Centre for Supercomputing at University of Bristol and cofounder of Isambard-AI. “It’s fitting that, for a climate-based project, the GPU hours used were relatively low, requiring less power from the supercomputer to run the workloads.” In addition to providing a look back at air pollution over the past year, the model can help predict future air pollution scenarios for the U.K. The team plans to further increase the resolution of its model by incorporating additional open data, enabling researchers to understand air pollution at street scale. The same generative pollution workflow also runs on the NVIDIA GB10 Grace Blackwell superchip-powered DGX Spark desktop AI system for inference and smaller training runs. Topping now has an DGX Spark system in his office retraining models. “You can now invest a few thousand dollars to get started developing powerful AI models,” Topping said. The team plans to release open source training data and workflows for the pollution models will be released so that similar models can be trained for other countries and regions. “Our aim is to offer this workflow to the entire world,” he said. “We hope that every global country and every major city with a small burst of supercomputer AI time will be able to produce their own detailed pollution models with their own local data.” Looking five years out, Topping sees the endpoint as something simpler still: an agentic interface where a clinician or government agency asks the question and the chain of models handles everything else. “With better open access to air quality observations, someone could ask our pollution model running on DGX Spark: what’s the pollution going to be like in this neighborhood tomorrow?” he said. “And a whole chain of interactions will deliver an answer, grounded on the science these frameworks represent.” Hear more from Topping in the webinar, AI for Science: From the Lab to the Frontier , taking place September 30. events.title: Saudi crown prince seeks Egypt’s backing as Houthi attacks rattle Red Sea oil routes
events.summary: Saudi Arabia’s crown prince is seeking backing from the president of Egypt, his ally across the Red Sea, as the kingdom faces increased attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels CAIRO -- Saudi Arabia’s crown prince sought backing Tuesday from the president of Egypt, his ally across the Red Sea, as the kingdom faces increased attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels on Saudi shipping and infrastructure that have helped drive a surge in global oil prices. Saudi Arabia has largely been on its own in confronting the Iranian-backed rebels, who rapidly captured more territory in Yemen over the past week and strengthened their ability to choke off Saudi oil exports out of the Red Sea. The vulnerability of the kingdom’s oil production was further underscored by an attack days ago that damaged its biggest pipeline. The strike was reportedly carried out by Iran’s allied militias in Iraq. It means the East-West Pipeline will be largely shut down for weeks as it is repaired, regional officials say, likely taking several million barrels of oil a day off the market. The Houthi offensive has opened up a new front in the Mideast’s war and boosted the hand of Iran, Saudi Arabia's traditional archrival in the region, which has attacked shipping through the region's other major maritime route, the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met in Cairo with Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi. The crown prince said in a statement that they both confirmed “their shared commitment to ensuring freedom and security of maritime navigation” in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the choke point at the sea’s southern end. El-Sissi's office put out a statement expressing “Egypt’s unwavering position in supporting Saudi Arabia.” Neither side gave firm details on any future steps. While Egypt is unlikely to offer military help to Saudi Arabia, the country is influential in the Arab world and can help rally support. Egypt has been at the center of mediation efforts in the last three years of turmoil in the region, keeping open relations with all parties, including Iran and its allies. In recent days, Houthi fighters made dramatic advances, seizing the Red Sea port of Mokha and three strategic islands in and near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The gains have further improved the Houthis’ position to seal off the strait to Saudi shipping, which they have been attacking since late July. Bab el-Mandeb connects the Red Sea to the open ocean and, from there, to Saudi Arabia’s biggest oil customers in Asia. Saudi Arabia has so far seemed reluctant to unleash a major military campaign against the Houthis, wary of bringing greater Houthi attacks on its oil infrastructure and being dragged back into an all-out civil war in Yemen, its southern neighbor. But as Houthi attacks continue, the kingdom faces a potential decision about whether to step up its military response or seek a diplomatic solution. Saudi military spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said its air defense forces intercepted and destroyed a drone Tuesday evening before it entered the airspace over Mecca, Islam’s holiest city and a focal point for followers of the faith. It’s the birthplace of Prophet Muhammad, where Muslims believe he first received God’s revelations of the Quran, and the location of the Kaaba, the black, cube-shaped structure that Muslims around the world turn to five times a day when praying. The security of the holy city is “a red line," he said, adding that Saudi forces will not hesitate to act against “hostile and terrorist behavior." The Houthis denied firing drones toward Mecca. The Saudis’ most essential ally, the United States, has been unpredictable and sometimes unreliable . U.S. President Donald Trump seems reluctant to widen an already unpopular and stalemated Mideast war ahead of congressional elections. The United Arab Emirates, previously a partner in the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis, has withdrawn from the war after conflicts between its allies in Yemen and Saudi Arabia’s. Yemen's U.N. Ambassador Abdullah Al-Saadi told the U.N. Security Council on Tuesday that Yemen’s armed forces are regrouping and regaining control but called for a U.N. arms embargo against the Houthis to be enforced and the council to condemn the escalation. He asked "whether the international community will accept for one of the world’s most important gateways for trade and energy to become a blackmail card in the hands of a transnational terrorist group.” Twin sisters conjoined at head underwent successful separation surgery: Hospital Judge blocks adding Trump tribute to Kennedy Center in scathing ruling Man arrested in death of woman found hanging from tree in Mississippi Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping during the war in Gaza led to a decrease in traffic through the Suez Canal, gouging Egypt’s revenues.

events.title: AI panic sparks rare bipartisan moment on Capitol Hill
events.summary: Lawmakers who want to regulate AI are doing something unusual as Congress barrels towards a lengthy recess with no tangible solution in sight: They're working across the aisle. Why it matters: Bipartisanship is increasingly elusive on Capitol Hill of late, but it remains a crucial first step for action in a Senate that requires 60 votes to pass most legislation. The latest example: Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) are pressing congressional leadership for a vote on their bill to establish a federal program to assess and monitor AI systems. "Recent incidents of rogue AI agent swarms hacking into public websites and systems have removed lingering doubts concerning the ability of these agents to wreak havoc on our cyber infrastructure," the pair wrote in a letter first obtained by Axios. "Congress cannot delay legislating to address frontier AI risks much longer. Industry-led evaluations are not enough." State of play: Several new bipartisan efforts to regulate AI have cropped up in the week since several current and former employees at Anthropic and OpenAI went public with concerns about the existential risks posed by their own products. Reps. Russell Fry (R-S.C.) and Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) are founding a caucus focused on AI small businesses, called the Innovators Caucus, as Axios reported Monday. Among the group's stated goals is starting work on a federal framework to regulate AI, as well as bringing small businesses to the AI policymaking table. The doomsday warnings have also breathed new life into existing bipartisan proposals to mitigate the dangers of AI. Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) has been publicly hawking his bill with Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) to require AI companies to include a human-activated "kill switch" in their systems. Lieu has also privately pitched Democratic leadership on creating a bipartisan AI select committee if they retake control of the House next year. Reps. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) and Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) have also been championing their comprehensive AI regulation bill, the Frontier Act. Zoom out: It has been years since Congress passed multiple pieces of truly big bipartisan legislation, and decades since bipartisan lawmaking on marquee issues was a regular practice. The most common moments when cross-party cooperation sees a renaissance on Capitol Hill these days: crises. Consider what got passed in the 117th Congress, on the heels of the Jan. 6 attack and the COVID pandemic: $1.2 trillion in infrastructure spending , a $280 billion semiconductor and research bill and the first major gun safety law in decades, all with bipartisan majorities. Yes, but: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has signaled that his chamber will not take any action on the AI front before the House leaves for a six-week recess that doesn't end until after Election Day. Johnson said in a CNN interview Sunday that Congress should "not smother American innovation" with overly burdensome AI regulations. President Trump has gone even further in dismissing the urgency of federal AI regulations, writing in a Truth Social post Monday: "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX." What to watch: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) has sounded a considerably more dire note on the issue. A potential House Democratic majority next year may be the place where AI regulation finally finds its footing on Capitol Hill.

events.title: Rep. Chuck Edwards files complaint against House Ethics
events.summary: Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) filed a complaint against the top Republican and Democrat on the House Ethics Committee on Tuesday, accusing the lawmakers who investigated him of breaking their own rules. Why it matters: Edwards is escalating his fight against the committee just two weeks after the House voted 413-2 to censure him over its findings that he violated House rules related to sexual harassment and a hostile workplace. Edwards' complaint asks the Office of Congressional Conduct to investigate Ethics Chair Michael Guest (R-Miss.) and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.) over their handling of his case. The Ethics Committee has previously disputed Edwards' account of the process. When it released its report last month, Guest and DeSaulnier said Edwards had agreed to waive certain procedural steps after reviewing a draft of the report several days earlier. The committee's findings follow Axios' reporting that Edwards singled out two young female staffers in their 20s for special attention that multiple sources described as inappropriate. Driving the news: "There was nothing ethical about this process," Edwards said in announcing the complaint. He alleges the committee circumvented its own rules by adopting its final report and recommending his censure before receiving his formal response. Edwards has maintained that his conduct did not violate House rules, though he did apologize to his wife, family, and the two women he allegedly harassed. The committee declined to comment. Catch up quick: The Ethics report's findings corroborated several anecdotes previously reported by Axios, including handwritten correspondence, personal gifts, drinking outings, and casino trips, and cited them as supporting evidence for its findings. He told one staffer that she had "written a complex chapter in my heart" shortly before she was set to leave his office in a three-page handwritten letter previously reported by Axios. Edwards gave the two young female staffers numerous gifts, including jewelry worth over $1,000, as well as "designer purses, guns , shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners," the Ethics panel found. What they're saying: "He has no remorse, and now he's trying to turn the tables and say somehow ethics did something wrong," Rep. Teresa Leger- Fernandez (D-NM), the chair of the Democratic Women's Caucus, told Axios. "It just shows you how hard to touch the man is," she added of Edwards. DeSaulnier told Axios he had not yet read Edwards' complaint but was confident the committee followed the proper process.

events.title: House GOP's Epstein files headache is back
events.summary: The Epstein files fight that consumed the House last year is threatening to engulf Republicans all over again. Why it matters: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is now just one Republican away from having the support he needs to force another politically painful Epstein vote — and he and his allies are hunting for the final GOP signature. Retiring Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) signed Massie's new discharge petition Monday, joining Massie and Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.). Massie and Mace told Axios they're actively targeting retiring Republicans and members in vulnerable districts for the fourth GOP signature that will get them the magic number to force a vote on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II. Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), one of four Republicans who bucked President Trump and GOP leadership to sign Massie's first Epstein petition last year, told Axios she's considering signing again and has been having conversations with Massie. The big picture: The push is reviving one of the most disruptive fights of Trump's second term for House Republicans. Last year's Epstein discharge petition became a months-long headache for Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and the White House before ultimately securing 218 signatures and forcing the issue onto the House floor. The bill passed with almost unanimous support in the House. The Epstein Files Transparency Act II would enforce and expand the release of remaining files at DOJ. "The Department of Justice continues to unlawfully withhold over 3 million Epstein files that should be released to the public. In addition, the DOJ is unlawfully maintaining heavy redactions on the files it is releasing," Massie wrote in a s tatement last month . Reality check: Even if Massie locks down the Republican support he needs this week, the House is set to leave Washington Thursday until after the November midterms, meaning any potential floor showdown would come post-election. Democrats also still need to provide the remaining signatures needed to reach the 218 required to discharge the bill, though Democratic leadership is encouraging members to sign on. Massie said he views that as just a logistical problem: "I haven't found any Democrat who's against it." Behind the scenes: Massie and Mace are focusing their recruitment efforts on Republicans who may have less to lose from crossing Trump. "I've got one hero slot left," Massie told Axios. Massie said he's talking to members in districts "where they're polling 10 points down," arguing they can either stay off the petition and risk losing anyway or sign it and make the issue part of their reelection pitch. Mace told Axios she is also "talking to Republicans who are leaving, and some Republican districts that we need to focus in on now." The intrigue: Boebert could provide the fourth Republican signature, but Massie says he doesn't expect the Republicans who took the political risk last year to do it again. "Anybody who did the first one is not obligated to put their head in the guillotine again," Massie said when asked about Boebert. "I think it's somebody else's turn." "Ralph Norman did it. He's a new one, and I think there are other new ones out there that we can get," he added. Between the lines: Massie is again accusing Johnson of manipulating the House calendar to deny him the time needed to force a vote. Johnson recently canceled two of the House's three remaining September workweeks. "He got a call from somebody that's above his pay grade that said, 'Take those two days off the calendar. Don't you dare give Massie the runway to get that plane off the ground,'" Massie said. Johnson, after calling Massie "stupid" for suggesting the House would add recess time, then formally moved to cancel session weeks, as Massie had predicted.

events.title: ‘Now We Can Know Everything and Do Anything,’ Jensen Huang Says at Dreamforce
events.summary: That was the message NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang brought to Salesforce Dreamforce Tuesday, joining CEO Marc Benioff onstage in an appearance that coincided with the announcement of Koa — Salesforce’s first CRM reasoning model, built on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super. Huang didn’t just take the stage. He walked into the crowd — threading through the audience at Moscone Center, mic in hand, with Benioff alongside. “We’re all following you, bro,” Benioff told Huang at one point, drawing applause. “With electricity, we could power everything,” Huang said, tracing the arc of industrial revolutions. “With the internet, you can find anything. And now, with artificial intelligence as an infrastructure layer across the planet, we can know everything and do anything.” That arc led directly to the announcement. Salesforce’s first reasoning model was built by post-training NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super on a proprietary synthetic dataset drawn from nearly three decades of enterprise CRM deployments. When Benioff asked Huang about AI safety, Huang was direct. “Safety is paramount in a lot of ways. It’s job one,” Huang said. “However, safety is an engineering problem. We’re developing computing systems after all … If you build a product or a service and you’re not confident in its functionality, capability or safety, then don’t release it.” He reiterated that innovation and leadership should coincide with safety and security . “Innovation, speed and safe products — it’s a false choice,” Huang said. “You could definitely have both at the same time. So run as fast as you can. But if you feel at any given point in time the company’s out of control, or the product’s not going to be safe, take a pause and make sure you get it right.” Throughout his talk, Huang offered a positive vision for the future of AI. He noted he was among the first to push back on the notion that AI would end the software industry. He also pushed back on the idea that AI is a threat to jobs. “As a result of our ambition, and with the productivity boost we get from AI, the sky’s the limit,” he added. “Engage AI. Don’t get left behind.” “Every company, every enterprise, every country would become an AI company,” Huang said. “It’s going to be an agentic enterprise.” “The sky is especially the limit for our Trailblazers,” Benioff said, referring to the company’s customer and developer community. “I think this technology, the way it empowers people … the technology can partner with them to do this in incredible new ways.” Because NVIDIA Nemotron is open, Salesforce was able to fine-tune and run the model entirely within its own infrastructure. Salesforce controls the weights, the model runs on Salesforce’s systems and no customer data is used during training or inference. “Not a single byte of customer data was used,” said Rohan Kumar, Salesforce’s president of platform and engineering, who introduced Koa before Huang took the stage. Open models went from 30% at the beginning of last year to now some 70%, Huang explained. “People are both adopting closed models at exponential rates, but also building their own custom AIs — because every single software company is an AI company, and every single enterprise is going to be an agentic and AI enterprise.” NVIDIA is one of them — running on Salesforce across sales, service, marketing and operations, and currently piloting Agentforce for customer-support workflows. Koa was built using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with NVIDIA NeMo RL, NeMo Gym and NeMo AutoModel. The training corpus covers synthetic enterprise scenarios across 14+ industries — manufacturing, financial services, healthcare and travel. In Salesforce’s CRM Bench, a model benchmark that includes a suite of real-world tasks like updating an opportunity, routing a case, or scheduling a follow-up, Koa already matches or exceeds leading model performance on CRM actions with 3x fewer errors. Koa is already running inside Salesforce, powering an employee agent in Slack, and is moving into customer pilots in October as a customer-selectable model in Agentforce, starting with Formula 1, UChicago Medicine, Baxter Credit Union, 1-800Accountant, Engine and Xero. General availability is expected winter 2026 in U.S. regions. events.title: How Ed Sheeran's tour imploded over a geopolitical fight
events.summary: Ed Sheeran's world tour spiraled into chaos this week after one opener was removed, every remaining opening act quit and stadiums threatened to pull the plug on the tour. Why it matters: The turmoil reveals the power dynamics behind major concert tours, showing how even a global star like Sheeran can be forced to take a back seat on decisions about his own shows. Driving the news: All four of Sheeran's remaining supporting acts announced Tuesday that they were dropping out. Irish musicians Aaron Rowe and Beoga , as well as Danish band Lukas Graham , said Tuesday they were leaving the tour. Rowe was set to replace Macklemore as the opener for the U.S. shows, AP reports. Finneas , who was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year, also announced he was exiting the concert series, saying on Instagram that "artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed." Catch up quick: The moves came one day after rapper Macklemore, who was scheduled for most of the remaining tour dates, was dropped after using his sets to voice support for Palestinians and condemn the war in Gaza during shows on Sept. 4-5 at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. Macklemore told the MetLife crowd on Sept. 4 that he wanted to do the tour so he could "say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine.'" His performance included images of war-torn Gaza playing on the video board. The tour's promoters, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone Monday that concert venues threatened to cancel shows unless Macklemore was dropped from the tour after his pro-Palestinian comments. Zoom in: Macklemore said the decision came after he spoke with Sheeran, alleging that the headliner faced pressure from stadium owners including Robert Kraft, owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium. According to Macklemore, Sheeran is typically "apolitical" and the recent round of backlash "challenged" him "in a way it never had before." The other side: Sheeran shared on Instagram Tuesday that the decision to remove Macklemore from the tour came not from him, but from the promoters. "I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living." Sheeran also wrote on Instagram that he didn't want his Loop Tour drawn into a public discussion around the war in Gaza. "I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," Sheeran wrote on IG. "The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy. There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated." He added: "I have my personal views on the devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care. Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own personal way." Zoom out: The turmoil over Sheeran's concert tour raises broader questions about political speech at concerts. As Rolling Stone notes, several stadiums that opposed Macklemore's appearance are publicly owned. One such venue is Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida, which faced calls to cancel Ye's shows earlier this year due to his past antisemitic comments. The bottom line: Sheeran has tried to keep politics off his stage. The fight over Gaza has now made that neutrality difficult to maintain.
