events.title: Top Oversight Dem Opens Investigation of Donald Trump Jr.’s Russian Oligarch-Funded Wedding
events.summary: Donald Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Trump, at an event at the White House in June. Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee launched an investigation into Donald Trump Jr.’s relationship with a Russian oligarch who paid for much of Trump Jr.’s wedding earlier this year. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., sent two letters on Monday to the White House and Trump Jr. requesting records related to Trump Jr.’s financial relationship with the oligarch, Umar Kremlev. “The secretive, close relationship between the son of a sitting U.S. President and a member of Russian dictator Vladimir Putin’s inner circle raises serious national security and public corruption concerns,” Garcia wrote. Garcia told Trump Jr. it “may be the most serious allegation against you to date.” The letter to Trump Jr. asked for documents including Trump Jr.’s communications with Kremlev and “financial records of all purchases made for your wedding by foreign nationals.” “Paper Trail” Podcast Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “ Paper Trail .” Trump Jr. did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Garcia’s investigation. The letters were prompted by a ProPublica investigation published Monday , which revealed that Kremlev secretly covered hundreds of thousands of dollars of expenses for Trump Jr.’s wedding. That included renting out a private island in the Bahamas for multiple nights. The wedding guest list numbered around 50, including Jared Kushner and other members of the Trump family. Kremlev, who first met Trump Jr. recently, also attended the intimate affair with a large group of other Russians. Kremlev is close to Putin and serves as the head of the International Boxing Association, a scandal-plagued sports group that has been financed by the Russian state-owned energy giant Gazprom. The wedding payments came from an IBA-affiliated entity in Dubai that the boxing association uses for financial transactions. Kremlev’s press office previously told ProPublica that he and Trump Jr. “have a friendly relationship” and that they don’t talk politics. After ProPublica’s story was published, Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Trump, released a joint statement confirming Kremlev’s role. “Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us,” they said in a statement published on her Instagram account. “It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful.” They added, “Friendship doesn’t require a political motive.” The couple also drew a distinction between the ceremony itself, which was just family, and the rest of the wedding weekend. In a statement released by the White House after the story was published, President Donald Trump echoed that. “I have no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day from the wedding,” he said. “It was an ‘afterparty’ given in their honor. Not a big deal!” The couple exchanged vows on Friday, May 22, on a private island in the Bahamas. The wedding festivities then continued for two days. The Saturday, May 23, event, which Kremlev paid for, was held on the same island as the ceremony. (“Night 2. One Love!” Bettina Trump posted about the Saturday festivities on Instagram.) The Sunday reception was held a roughly 10-minute boat ride away on a neighboring private island, rented out by Kremlev. At the Sunday reception, the couple had their first dance, with Bettina Trump wearing her wedding dress, and ate a five-tier wedding cake topped with a miniature bride and groom.  Afterward, the couple’s wedding planner talked to Hello! magazine about planning the three-day affair with Bettina Trump. “She wanted a progression,” said the planner, Lewis Miller. “The ceremony was very serene and pretty and soft, and the dinner was very elegant, and then the next night was much more colorful, and then the last night was more kind of cool and fun tropical vibes.” Read More Donald Trump Jr.’s Bahamas Wedding Was Secretly Bankrolled by Russian Oligarch Close to Putin The post Top Oversight Dem Opens Investigation of Donald Trump Jr.’s Russian Oligarch-Funded Wedding appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: House quashes another Trump impeachment push with Dem help
events.summary: The House voted for the third time in two years to quash a rogue effort by Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) to impeach President Trump. Why it matters: As with the last two times, the vote divided House Democrats. Some sided with Green, but others voted "present" or actively helped GOP leadership defeat the effort. Green frustrated his Democratic colleagues by forcing the vote without support from party leadership, with one telling Axios the move was "fucked up." The Texas Democrat defended his attempts to impeach Trump over killings committed by federal immigration officials, calling it a "life and death" matter. Driving the news: The House voted 232-147 for Republican leadership's measure to table — effectively, kill — Green's motion to force a vote on impeaching Trump, with 47 members voting "present." Between the lines: Some Democrats who voted with Green privately sneered before the vote that it was a distraction from party messaging on the House's last in-session week before the midterm. Green pushed back by saying the lawmakers who criticized him "don't have the courage to stand up and face me" and challenging them to debate the matter publicly.

events.title: Crypto industry’s top legislative priority implodes
events.summary: The cryptocurrency industry just lost the lead of a lifetime. Just last year, banks were so terrified of digital asset companies’ war chest that they scrambled to overhaul their own lobbying . But on Tuesday, senators failed to advance the firms’ top legislative priority, shrugging off the threat of tens of millions of dollars that still could hit them this fall . President Donald Trump’s crypto adviser had hoped for Republican unity , but even that couldn’t materialize, as baked-in allegiance to banks drove three Republicans to vote no; all Democrats voted no out of concern the bill wouldn’t rein in Trump. Odds are high lawmakers won’t take up another permanent overhaul of crypto regulation until Trump leaves office. “The amount of money the crypto industry spent on lobbying firms for such a staggering defeat would have been better spent curing cancer,” one lobbyist told Semafor after the vote. — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board votes to close building
events.summary: The Kennedy Center's board voted Tuesday to close the iconic performing arts center's main building for a renovation project championed by President Trump , multiple outlets reported and a source familiar confirmed to Axios. Why it matters: Trump's attempts to put his name on the building , which memorializes former President John F. Kennedy, have fueled an ongoing legal and political battle. The decision came hours after a federal judge again said the center could not put Trump's name on the building . Driving the news: Trump said in a Truth Social post that the renovation "cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board's approved name." He said that if the ruling is not in his allies' favor or is not overturned by the Supreme Court , "the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place." Catch up quick: A resolution from the board, filed in the ongoing legal fight with Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over the Center, cited "water intrusion and deterioration of the center's physical plant" that it said "caused a partial ceiling collapse," arguing the safety risk "greatly outweighs any reputational risk associated with closing the main building." A second resolution filed in the case listed ways Trump could be "legally and appropriately recognized" on the building, after a federal judge ruled that only Congress can change its name. Zoom out: The resolution states that without his name on the building, it's "unlikely" Trump "will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building." It listed options for text on the exterior marble beneath the center's name, including "A Legacy protected through the Generosity of President Donald J. Trump" or "Renovation, Restoration, and support by President Donald J. Trump." Friction point: U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper blocked the center from closing earlier this year, finding that "the Board was derelict in discharging the full range of its responsibilities to the Center" and "based its decision on an insufficient, one-sided presentation of information." But in that order, he said his injunction would not prevent "capital repair work," nor would it "categorically prohibit the Board from closing the Center should it come to this decision anew after independently balancing its multiple obligations to the Center in a prudent fashion." Catch up quick: The renovation project would address issues like corrosion and rehabilitating the building's iconic theaters and Grand Foyer, Axios previously reported. The draft resolution proposes sending marquee events offsite, while continuing some programming at the REACH — an indoor–outdoor space. Beyond infrastructure renovations, Trump ally and board member Paolo Zampolli outlined his luxury vision for the space to Axios' Cuneyt Dil, including expanding the outdoor park to create a "concert hub," and building a marina. What we're watching: For now, those ideas aren't part of the board's resolution — but the center's future under Trump remains in flux, in part because of an ongoing legal challenge to the president's takeover. And while Trump allies position him as the center's financial savior, the Washington Post reported that ticket sales plunged after the board of trustees voted to name the center after him. events.title: Helping voters navigate election information in the age of AI
events.summary: 2026 midterm elections: Helping voters navigate election information in the age of AI Sep 15, 2026 | By Ginny Badanes, General Manager, Tech for Society, Microsoft As Americans prepare to vote this November, artificial intelligence is changing how many people find and understand election information. Some voters are deliberately turning to AI tools with questions about candidates, ballot measures, election procedures, and issues that matter to their communities. Others are encountering AI-generated summaries at the top of search results. In either case, AI is increasingly becoming a front door to election information. This shift is happening quickly. More than 30% of the U.S. working-age population now uses AI (Microsoft AI Diffusion Index, Q1 2026; Microsoft, AI Adoption Across the United States ) . These tools can help people understand complicated topics, compare information, and explore unfamiliar issues. But election information can also present some challenges for AI. It is highly local, changes quickly, and can be incomplete, contested, or stripped of essential context. The answer is not to steer voters away from AI, it is to help people use it wisely, particularly when the information may influence aspects of their voting experience, such as how, when, and where they cast their ballot. That is why, on National Voter Registration Day , a day when our brands and products come together to encourage civic participation , we’re launching the next phase of our voter education initiative, Check. Recheck. Vote . This year, the campaign will equip voters with practical AI literacy skills for the 2026 election season. We launched Check. Recheck. Vote. in 2024 to help voters recognize the risks posed by deceptive AI-generated content. Deepfakes and other deceptive media remain a serious concern. But in conversations with voters and election organizations, we are also hearing about a broader and more immediate challenge. Millions of people now encounter election information through AI-generated answers, and many are not sure how to determine whether those answers are current, complete, or reliable. The updated campaign gives voters three straightforward steps: Check the sources and citations behind an AI-generated answer. Look for where the information came from, who published it, and when it was last updated. Be cautious when an answer provides no sources. Recheck important details by visiting the original sources and comparing what other credible sources say. This is especially important for fast-changing or location-specific information. Vote based on current information from your state or local election website, including official guidance on registration, voting options, deadlines, and polling locations. At the center of the campaign is a new 75-second video that shows how an AI-generated answer can appear during an ordinary election-related search, explains where these answers can fall short, and offers simple steps voters can take before relying on them. The campaign website pairs the video with practical guidance and links to authoritative election resources, including state-by-state voting information and tools for educators. We are working with the National Association of Secretaries of State (NASS) and the National Association of State Election Directors (NASED) to scale the reach of this campaign across all fifty states and the territories and to point voters to accurate information directly from state and local election officials so they can participate with confidence. We believe that civics and voter education start well before a citizen is old enough to vote. That’s why we are also investing in efforts to extend AI voter literacy education in the classroom. The campaign website includes a classroom activity to help students examine how AI may shape the election information they encounter, practice verifying claims, and keep their own judgment at the center of the process. We are also amplifying our impact on this important issue by supporting the News Literacy Project . We’re also proud to announce today that, in partnership with iCivics, we are launching Village Square – a new Minecraft Education civic learning experience that helps students explore how communities make decisions and solve shared challenges. The game brings concepts such as dialogue, participation, and collective decision-making to life through immersive gameplay. Village Square gives educators and families an engaging, nonpartisan way to help young people practice listening to different perspectives, weighing trade-offs and working together to build stronger communities. Finally, we know that credible local reporting remains essential to informed civic participation, and that reporting is under strain in many communities. In Washington state, Microsoft is partnering with the Associated Press Fund for Journalism to expand election coverage for 10 local newsrooms operating 14 news websites. Participating newsrooms receive access to AP election results and race calls, vote tabulations, state-specific maps and graphics, and resources that help local journalists connect national and statewide developments to the communities they serve. The newsrooms represent communities from Seattle to Spokane and the Wenatchee Valley. Their work complements the reporting of the Associated Press, helping trusted, fact-based election coverage and results reach communities that might otherwise lack access. This investment reflects a broader reality. Voters need more than information. They need reliable sources that can provide context, ask hard questions, correct mistakes, and explain what national developments mean at the local level. Microsoft’s Support for the 2026 Midterms Voters aren’t the only ones navigating this AI moment, so are the people running campaigns and conducting elections, all while facing an increasingly complex cybersecurity landscape. Microsoft has long supported the security and resilience of campaigns and elections. In 2018, we launched AccountGuard to help political campaigns and democracy-focused organizations defend against cyberattacks, and during the 2024 election cycle we joined dozens of other technology companies in the Tech Accord to Combat Deceptive Use of AI in 2024 Elections . Here’s how that commitment continues today: Equipping election officials. With The Elections Group, International IDEA, Ready for Tuesday and Arizona State University’s Mechanics of Democracy Lab, we launched the free, open-source AI + Elections Skills Hub : prompts, sample AI agents, and draft policies for responsible adoption. It’s already reached 1,000+ officials across 45 states. Strengthening cybersecurity. We’ve deployed Microsoft Sentinel to several state and local election offices for stronger threat detection, and we’re also supporting select election and political stakeholders with MDASH to find and fix software vulnerabilities faster. Countering bomb hoaxes.

events.title: Scoop: Trump pollster gives GOP a data center survival guide
events.summary: President Trump's longtime pollster is offering Republican candidates a detailed playbook for neutralizing Democratic attacks over AI data centers — down to what language they should and shouldn't use. Why it matters: Republican strategists say GOP candidates have been all over the map in responding to the backlash to data centers. The goal is to put Republicans on offense after months of playing defense on the issue. Driving the news: Pollster Tony Fabrizio warns in a two-page memo obtained by Axios that "unqualified support for building more AI data centers is a losing position." Fabrizio specifically advises candidates not to say, "I support building more data centers," warning: "It will be clipped and show up in ads." Instead, he tells Republicans to support AI infrastructure only if developers pay for their own power needs, protect consumers from higher utility bills and safeguard local water and natural resources. Fabrizio argues that candidates must make clear those conditions are enforceable, rather than voluntary commitments from tech companies. "This converts the candidate from a defender of technology companies into the person imposing rules on them," Fabrizio writes in the memo, which was sent Monday. Fabrizio offers a three-step script for candidates. First, "validate" voters' concerns about higher utility bills, the power grid and water use. Second, "draw the line" by vowing not to support projects that force families to subsidize them or allow tech companies to harm surrounding communities. Finally, argue that projects should move forward only if companies provide their own power, protect ratepayers and safeguard local water. "The order matters," Fabrizio writes. "It adopts voters' concerns as the approval standard instead of asking them to set those concerns aside." Fabrizio warns against generic support for "more data centers," leading with jobs or China, dismissing local concerns or defending individual projects before their costs and resource demands are known. By the numbers: Fabrizio's polling shows voters are far more receptive to data center construction with conditions than unrestricted development. Sixty-one percent of registered voters favor allowing construction with conditions, compared with 28% who favor prohibiting data centers altogether. His polling also finds voters oppose additional data center construction without conditions by 65% to 24%. The background: Fabrizio is a central player in Trump's midterm political operation, helping shape the polling and strategy guiding the GOP's campaign to retain control of Congress. Yes, but: Trump remains an enthusiastic booster of data centers even as Republicans grapple with growing voter concerns about their local impact. "I'm telling you, it's all a hoax. The data centers are great, and they make people wealthy, and they make states wealthy, and it's the oil of the next 20, 25 years," Trump said Monday.

events.title: Trump considered dangerous, corrupt by majority in new poll
events.summary: Data: The Economist/YouGov ; Chart: Avery Lotz A slight majority of registered voters describe President Trump as corrupt and dangerous, a recent poll found, while just 14% say he isn't divisive. The big picture: Simply put, polling hasn't been pretty for the president — or for his Iran war , tariffs or other top priorities . Still, with the midterms weeks away, Trump has centered himself, making the election a referendum on his presidency . By the numbers: " Corrupt" (53%) and "dangerous" (51%) led the list of descriptors voters applied to Trump in the Sept. 11-14 The Economist-YouGov poll of 1,461 U.S. registered voters. Those words were followed by "out-of-touch" (47%), "cruel" (46%) and "bold" (45%). Just 18% said they'd use the word "steady" to describe the president. Worth noting: Democrats are testing an anti-corruption midterm message as Americans' perceptions of government corruption hit a 20-year high , per Gallup's trend , and polls show Americans believe the president has inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency while in office. The results broke sharply by party — 91% of Democrats and 62% of independents said Trump was corrupt, compared with 10% of Republicans. Republicans weren't universally positive: Less than half (49%) said they'd use the word "honest" to describe the president. Just 10% said it didn't describe him, while 41% had no opinion. Similarly, 38% of Republicans said he was steady, while 53% said they had no opinion. What they're saying: White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in an emailed statement that "President Trump has launched an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government, holding criminals accountable and saving taxpayers billions of dollars." Ingle also accused Democrats in Congress of failing to stop waste, fraud and abuse in government. Zoom out: Trump's approval rating ticked up from the lowest point of his political career, recorded last month in Reuters-Ipsos' trend , this month. Some 35% of Americans approved of his performance, up from 33% in the late August poll, per Reuters. Between the lines: The last thing many Republicans want, Axios' Marc Caputo reports , is for Trump to make the midterms a vote on his popularity (or lack thereof). Still, Trump headlined both nights of the party's midterm convention in Dallas and pledged a $5,000 dividend to every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans keep control of Congress — a plan that would cost more than $1 trillion. Friction point: YouGov's polling found that a majority signaled they believe it's unlikely Trump actually follows through with the idea, which Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has said would require congressional approval. More than four in 10 (41%) said he definitely wouldn't do it, while an additional 16% said he probably wouldn't. More said it was a bad idea (45%) than those who said it was a good idea (38%). Methodology: This Economist-sponsored poll was taken September 11-14, 2026. Respondents were selected from YouGov's opt-in panel to be representative of adult U.S. citizens, and screened for voter registration. The margin of error is ± 3.3%. Go deeper: Even some Republican voters sour on Trump

events.title: How the Copilot Creators Collective is shaping the future of creativity and AI literacy
events.summary: The New Media Movement: How the Copilot Creators Collective is Shaping the Future of Creativity and AI Literacy A year ago, Microsoft brought together a group of Filipino creators around a shared question: what becomes possible when creativity, community, and AI come together? That question became the starting point for the Copilot Creators Collective, a community built around a clear mission: to help more Filipinos understand, explore, and use AI responsibly through the voices of creators they trust. One year later, that mission has been brought to life by CCC members who are not only experimenting with Microsoft Copilot in their own work, but also translating AI into stories, conversations, and learning moments that feel practical, familiar, and human. At the heart of the Collective is Microsoft’s vision of empowering every person and organization on the planet to achieve more. For the CCC, that vision extends from creators to the communities they reach. Through campaigns, learning sessions, and creator-led storytelling, members have helped broaden AI literacy and advocate for responsible AI use by showing how Copilot can support real moments in work, life, education, creativity, and learning. “Over the past year, the Copilot Creators Collective has shown us what happens when Filipino creators are given the space, tools, and community to explore AI with purpose,” said Josh Aquino, Head of Communication of Microsoft Philippines. “But the Collective was never built for creators alone. It was built so more Filipinos could see AI in the context of everyday life—through people they trust, stories they relate to, and examples that show how Copilot can help them create, learn, work, and solve problems responsibly.” One Year of Learning, Experimenting, and Creating Together In its first year, the CCC’s mission moved from idea to action through the creators who carried it into different communities. Across learning spaces, workplace conversations, and education campaigns, members helped make AI feel less abstract and more useful to the people it was meant to serve. At the YSEALI Bootcamp for Digital Creators, Isa Rodriguez, CJ Salvador, and Jax Reyes brought creator-led perspectives to a regional initiative designed to equip young Southeast Asian leaders with digital storytelling and responsible technology skills. Organized in partnership with the U.S. Department of State through the Young Southeast Asian Leaders Initiative, the bootcamp gathered 81 Attendees from across the region, representing multiple nations and communities. The initiative provided a platform for CCC members to show how Microsoft 365 and Copilot can support productivity, content creation, and responsible experimentation. Their participation showed how AI literacy can start with people who understand the realities of digital storytelling and can speak to peers in a way that feels grounded, practical, and approachable. That same role came through in Microsoft’s Work Trend Index campaign, which emphasized that while AI is already embedded in everyday work, the next frontier is helping people and organizations turn individual experimentation into trusted, repeatable, and scalable ways of working. Through this campaign, Trixie Esguerra-Bugia helped make insights on AI adoption, productivity, and the future of work more relatable for everyday professionals and creators. Her own use of Copilot reflects the practical value she helps audiences see: it supports the behind-the-scenes work that makes content creation possible, from organizing shot lists to checking grammar and refining outlines. For creators working as one-human teams, she shows how AI can serve as a digital assistant that brings more structure and confidence to everyday work. In education, Alvin Santos and Reb Atadero helped bring the same message to Filipino teachers and learners through Microsoft’s campaign in partnership with the Department of Education. Leveraging DepEd’s nationwide network, the campaign showed how free tools such as Copilot Chat and Reading Progress can address classroom needs at scale. In just 21 weeks, it reached 3,431 students across eight regions, analyzed 8,381 reading submissions, trained 2,002 teachers, and achieved 91.5 percent teacher satisfaction. By connecting AI to everyday teaching, literacy, and student support, Alvin and Reb helped frame it as a practical aid for educators and learners alike. Alvin’s own experience reinforces this point: he has used Copilot as a creative sounding board and to develop lesson plans tailored to French non-native English speakers. The Collective’s work also shows how AI can support more ambitious ideas behind the scenes. Ceej Tantengco-Malolos experienced this while organizing an art exhibit for women’s sports. With Copilot and a small team, she created display mockups, drafted media invitations, and built a promotional plan for an event that might have otherwise felt difficult to take on. Her example adds another layer to the CCC’s first-year story: responsible AI is not only about learning the tool, but using it to bring meaningful ideas to life. Other members of the Collective echo this sense of possibility. Buji Babiera shared how Copilot helped him gather themes from different parts of the world for a local story under a tight deadline. Abi Maravilla described Copilot as a sounding board that helps simplify the complex and organize ideas without becoming overwhelmed. Andi Lopez shared how it helps turn scattered thoughts into something clearer and more meaningful, while also supporting work such as marketing pitch decks and data analysis for esports commentary. Seen together, these efforts move the CCC’s story forward from experimentation to impact. In its first year, the Collective helped broaden AI literacy by meeting Filipinos where they are: creators learning to work more efficiently, professionals navigating the future of work, educators looking for practical classroom support, and communities discovering how AI can help them start, organize, teach, create, and solve problems more responsibly. One year in, the Copilot Creators Collective stands as both a milestone and a starting point. Its first year shows how Filipino creators are already using AI to work more efficiently, think more expansively, and tell stories with greater confidence. It also shows that the future of creativity will not be shaped by technology alone. It will be shaped by people: creators who ask better questions, share what they learn, and use new tools to bring more thoughtful ideas into the world. “My first year with the Copilot Creator Collective was marked with remarkable firsts. It was my first time working with Microsoft Copilot and AI in general” said Alvin Santos. “And also, my first to be part of a project that fostered long-lasting partnerships with the brand and a thoughtfully curated bunch of amazing content creators. I’m raring to see what’s in store for the 2nd year!

events.title: New AI tool lets influencers ‘scale themselves like software’
events.summary: The News The tech-focused creator Emily Higgins is speaking directly into the camera about the importance of a good hook for a social media video — she does what looks like three takes, each with a slightly different script. But Higgins only filmed one video. The other two were AI-edited, using a new tool from New York-based tech-media startup Avail that allows brands to create dozens of variants of video ads recorded by human influencers. The creatorAPI platform, which launched Tuesday, points to a social-media future in which content created or augmented with AI is increasingly common. It’s also a response to the rise of so-called “synthetic influencers,” completely fake avatars that can hawk goods on the internet. Instead, the tool will allow creators to “scale themselves like software,” said Avail CEO Chris Giliberti. It’s designed so the human creator authorizes all of their different videos: Brands can fix recording mistakes, test out different intros, or create variations that target different geographies or audiences. Using a technique known as “dark posting,” all the different ads won’t show up on the creator’s profile, but will proliferate into users’ feeds. Avail put together a cocktail of third-party AI models to create the tool. Know More Giliberti acknowledged the tool could be controversial, given how difficult it is for an untrained eye to tell the differences between AI-edited videos and the growing public pushback to anything tinged with AI, especially in the creative space. “There’s this purity that people expect from creatives, like they’re always the last people that are allowed to adopt productivity tools,” he said. “I just think it’s really unfortunate that software engineers are able to crank out 10 times more code with [AI] tools and that’s palatable... but the second a creator adopts a tool like this, they’re shamed for it.” Notable As the technology improves, using AI to edit video for translation purposes is increasingly common: Amazon last week rolled out alternate-language versions of a popular German soap opera that were made using AI lip-dubbing.

events.title: Slowing AI development could boost hyperscaler balance sheets
events.summary: Any slowdown in AI spending would let hyperscalers catch their financial breath and ease their reliance on borrowing to fund their buildouts. A Semafor review of analyst estimates finds that at current projections, as tracked by S&P Capital IQ, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, and Microsoft are expected to spend $66 billion more on capital spending (nearly all of it AI-related) than they earn in cash from operations over the next six quarters. Debt, stock sales, and complex deals that shift that spending off their balance sheets are filling the gap. Even a 10% pullback in capex flips that to a $74 billion surplus; a 20% pullback puts them more than $200 billion in the black. These companies might still choose to tap outside funding — “always spend other people’s money” remains a cardinal rule of corporate finance — but they wouldn’t be forced to. They could spend some time rebuilding balance sheets that have become stretched by breakneck spending or restoring stock buybacks that have largely been sacrificed on the AI altar. — Jake Angelo

events.title: AI is doing what Wall Street couldn't
events.summary: Liz’s view Chuck Prince, CEO of Citigroup from 2003 to 2007, is remembered for one quote that captured the greed and spinelessness of Wall Street bosses chasing riches while steering the global economy toward a cliff: “As long as the music is playing, you’ve got to get up and dance. We’re still dancing.” (Prince later clarified that his comments were about private-equity buyouts, not subprime mortgages, but they became indelibly attached to the production of toxic housing bonds.) Today’s music is AI, not subprime mortgages, and it’s still playing. But this crop of Chuck Princes seems willing to consider stepping off the dance floor. I’m still not sure what Dario Amodei’s idea to “pace the frontier” actually means in practice — slower Wi-Fi at the Anthropic office? Tying the developers’ shoelaces together? — but it’s clearly a warning issued at the cost of some short-term riches, which is more than Prince ever managed. Prince knew how dangerous Wall Street’s subprime addiction was but couldn’t quit. Some peers knew too, and quietly did: JPMorgan began exiting subprime lending in late 2006, and Goldman Sachs’ strong-arm collateral demands ensured it was not stuck holding what Jeremy Irons’ Dick Fuld-esque character in the film would later call “the biggest bag of odorous excrement ever assembled in the history of capitalism.” Both firms paced their own frontiers. Neither did anything to stop the overall machine. The loudest alarms back then came from outsiders — misfit investors like Michael Burry and academics like Raghuram Rajan — who got plenty of grief for their candor . The calls this time are coming from inside the house. Notable Read Amodei’s full essay , calling on AI labs to “ pace the frontier. ”

events.title: AI biotech Isomorphic Labs is not slowing down, exec says
events.summary: The News Not all AI companies want to slow down. Chris Butler, who runs drug discovery at Isomorphic Labs, the Google-backed drug company started by DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis, pushed back against the suggestion that calls by OpenAI, Anthropic, and other AI leaders to pace the frontier would slow his company down. “We’re able to still progress regardless of what decisions are made elsewhere,” Butler said at the Semafor Future of Health Forum on Tuesday. “All of our AI models are locked down and locked down in-house,” he added. “So, really, for us, it’s about, how do we use the models that we’ve built internally to help to accelerate the drug discovery process.” Isomorphic, which was founded in 2021 as a DeepMind spinoff, raised $2.1 billion in its latest funding round in May, led by Thrive Capital, at an undisclosed valuation. It’s planning on plunging that money to help build out its pipeline and evolve its overall drug design; its drug discovery team is growing, with particular interest in oncology and immunology. “It is really important that we continue to see that progress toward the clinic,” he told Semafor’s healthcare reporter David Lim. Know More Butler said the company is “on track” and moving “smoothly” through preclinical development efforts. The company is also collaborating with Novartis, Eli Lilly, and Johnson & Johnson. Butler declined to provide more details on the timeline for clinical trials. Isomorphic is also trying to navigate the process of working with regulators about how it is using AI to accelerate drug development, Butler said. “That landscape is shifting to a point where the AI approach and bringing more data to help to guide what development programs could look like is growing.” “That’s got to be a partnership for us with the agency as we’re bringing molecules forward to know exactly what that looks like and help us work together with them. To bring that forward and to be able to decide what is needed, what needs expansion on, what is helpful in terms of working through the regulatory process and ultimately submission,” he added. As regulators look to shrink the length of time spent on drug discovery, Isomorphic is betting on a way to quickly transition from discovery to early stage clinical trials.

events.title: Cassidy warns time running out to fix Social Security
events.summary: The News Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., called on Congress to act on two issues before his term ends: the looming financial problems facing Social Security and the ballooning cost of healthcare. At Semafor’s Future of Health Forum on Tuesday, Cassidy, who is leaving the Senate at the end of the year, told Semafor’s Burgess Everett that a bipartisan effort is underway to address Social Security, but acknowledged that the window for Congress to act is narrowing. He pointed to the 2026 Social Security Trustees Report, released in June, which found that the program’s retirement trust fund would become insolvent in 2032 — triggering automatic benefit cuts of more than 20% unless Congress acts. Cassidy said that warning, combined with rising bond yields, has attracted renewed attention in Washington to a problem he has been trying to fix for six years. “The fact that I’ve been working on it for six years and I’ve got three months left and we’re having this conversation shows you how difficult it is,” Cassidy said. “On the other hand, the actuary report that came out a month or so ago, I think, helped sharpen people’s minds that we really have a problem.” Cassidy said the effort has bipartisan roots, pointing to a previous agreement involving seven Republicans and seven Democrats that he said was brought to President Joe Biden. He also referenced his current efforts with Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill, to pass The PROMISE Act. “Obviously, the window is closing. But the longer you wait to fix Social [Security], the worse it gets. And it doesn’t just get worse marginally,” Cassidy said. “I’m hoping against hope that we can do it. And if not, I’m looking for someone to pass it off to, and they will continue it next time.” Earlier this year, Cassidy lost his primary to a Republican challenger backed by President Donald Trump. Know More As chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, Cassidy also pointed to health care affordability as another area where he hopes Congress can make progress before he leaves office. He highlighted the bipartisan Patient Deserve Price Tags Act, which he said would give patients more information about the cost of medical services before receiving care. “If you think about it, healthcare is one of the few things in which you don’t know how much it’s going to cost when you walk in the door. And there’s a deliberate effort to obfuscate for the consumer how much something costs,” Cassidy said. “I think it’s a pretty good stab at trying to make healthcare more affordable.”

events.title: Massie moves to impeach Pete Hegseth over Iran War
events.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced a resolution Tuesday to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , accusing him of defying Congress and illegally continuing the U.S. war in Iran. Why it matters: The impeachment effort is a long shot in the GOP-controlled Congress, but Massie's resolution is privileged, meaning he can force a full House vote and put Republicans on the record over Hegseth's handling of the Iran war. It's a dramatic escalation in the retiring lawmaker's months-long push to rein in the Trump administration's war powers. Massie did not give GOP leaders a heads-up on his plans. The effort also comes after the House has repeatedly voted on efforts to constrain the administration's military campaign in Iran, including passing war powers resolutions in June and July directing the president to end U.S. hostilities with Tehran. The House is slated to vote Tuesday on another war powers resolution on the Iran war effort. Driving the news: Massie's resolution accuses Hegseth of carrying out orders to continue operations in Iran despite Congress' constitutional authority over war and its votes seeking to end the conflict. Massie argued Hegseth's actions "frustrated Congress's ability to exercise its most solemn constitutional responsibility" and allowed an "unlawful war" to continue. "In all of this, Secretary Hegseth has acted in a manner contrary to his trust as Secretary of Defense," Massie said on the House floor. The eight-article resolution also targets Hegseth over U.S. military operations in Venezuela and Yemen, including accusing him of illegally directing the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization. Zoom out: Hegseth already faced a separate impeachment push from House Democrats, who introduced six articles against him in April that included allegations he waged an unauthorized war against Iran. What's next: The House will have to take up the legislation within the next two legislative days, but GOP leaders could also move to vote on tabling the resolution instead. Editor's note: This story has been updated to say that Massie didn't let GOP leaders know in advance about his plans.

events.title: Kennedy Center's attempt to put Trump's name on building blocked again by judge
events.summary: A federal judge ruled Tuesday that the Kennedy Center's latest attempt to put President Trump's name on the performing arts center violated his earlier order blocking its renaming . The big picture: The order came just before the Kennedy Center's board, now composed of Trump loyalists, is set to weigh shutting down the building for renovations that members argue must include Trump being "appropriately recognized" on the structure. Driving the news: While Trump allies have argued the latest attempt to recognize Trump does not violate the law, U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper said "[l]inguistic gymnastics cannot extricate the Kennedy Center's Board from an operative judicial order or the governing statute it was designed to enforce." Cooper ordered for Trump's name to be removed from the building in May, saying only Congress could change the name of the center that memorializes President John F. Kennedy. The judge blocked the center from putting an inscription that read "renovated and restored by Donald J. Trump" on the main building or renaming the campus the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza." Cooper wrote, "Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing." Catch up quick: The board voted last month to again add Trump's name to the building to recognize his renovation push in an apparent attempt to circumvent Cooper's prior ruling. The fresh attempt wouldn't change the building's name. Rather, it would put an inscription under the Kennedy Center sign acknowledging Trump and rename the surrounding plaza after him. Zoom in: A recent draft resolution from the board, filed in federal court by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), stated that "without such appropriate recognition" it's "unlikely" that Trump would "provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building." It proposed several options for "public recognitions" of the president to be placed on the exterior marble beneath the center's name. Cooper noted in his order, however, that "the government offered 'no proof that current or future donations hinge on President Trump's name being on the building'." What he's saying: Trump argued in a Tuesday Truth Social post that the center "is in a virtual state of collapse" and argued the board knows he's the "only one" who can save it "because I have the ability to raise the money, and the ability to construct — that few others have." The board will meet today, where they could decide to shut the building down. Go deeper: Kennedy Center could close today. This Trump ally has big ideas.

events.title: From Megawatts to Tokens: How NVIDIA Maximizes AI Factory Production
events.summary: On a sweltering August evening in Silicon Valley, as the sun dropped and air conditioning loads spiked , Silicon Valley Power sent a signal to an AI factory to adjust its power consumption. Varun Sivaram was watching on Zoom with about forty others — his team at Emerald AI in their San Francisco conference room, engineers at the data center and people from the utility itself. Nobody touched anything. Emerald AI’ s Conductor platform — a grid-orchestration platform from NVIDIA partner Emerald AI, and an early example of the kind of flexibility NVIDIA DSX Flex is built to deliver — receives signals about grid conditions and adjusts the data center’s flexible computing workloads. Work that can wait is slowed or rescheduled, while higher-priority services continue operating. The goal is to reduce electricity demand when the grid is constrained without interrupting critical AI workloads— exactly what Silicon Valley Powe r needed, When the reduction showed on screen, everyone cheered. “We were watching with bated breath,” Sivaram said. “It was our first time deploying across thousands of NVIDIA GPUs.” His head of product, Mansi Shah, was emotional. “This feels kind of like a SpaceX rocket launch,” she said. Silicon Valley Power h as since sent more than 200 demand signals to that AI factory. It worked every single time. This is grid flexibility in production. And it points at something much bigger than one facility in Santa Clara: a path to unlocking the power America’s AI factories need, without waiting a decade to build new transmission lines. At the AI Infra Summit on Tuesday, Ian Buck, NVIDIA’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, made AI factory efficiency the centerpiece of his infrastructure keynote. Results from cloud provider Lambda’s first validation in a deployment environment, released the same day, put numbers to it: a fixed power budget can support 24% more token throughput when managed intelligently. “With our proof of concept, we believe we’ve moved beyond the limitation of fixed power budgets,” said Dave Ward, president of cloud services at Lambda . “NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS paves the way to reclaiming stranded capacity and converting it into real-world usage, with significantly more compute density in the same footprint.” That August evening, when SVP called, Conductor executed against a predefined workload hierarchy: lowest-priority jobs yielded, high-priority inference kept running, and power fell from four megawatts to three. Automated. No operator required. In the AI factory economy, power is the constraint. Work per gigawatt is the metric. Data center operators are meticulous about efficiency — every watt put to work is a watt delivering productive compute, and the industry has driven remarkable gains at every layer of the stack, from facility design to rack-level power conversion. DSX extends that discipline into the AI workload itself. Smarter rack provisioning puts power where workloads actually need it. Operational intelligence — tighter scheduling, faster restarts, leaner checkpointing — keeps GPUs running rather than waiting. The goal is the same one operators have always pursued: more work from the power you have. “A one-gigawatt factory will never become a two-gigawatt factory,” NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang has said. The answer engineers reach when systems hit physical limits is always the same: stop optimizing the parts and start designing the whole. Introduced at GTC Taipei in May, NVIDIA DSX is that answer for the AI factory — and the early deployments are already proving it out. The full platform spans networking, cooling, water efficiency and facility design; the sections below focus on some of the results so far in power management and grid participation. More Compute, Same Budget: DSX MaxLPS Lambda’s results, released at the AI Infra Summit, are the first validation of DSX MaxLPS on NVIDIA HGX B20 0 GPU Servers. DSX MaxLPS monitors GPU and rack-level power consumption and reallocates headroom across nodes based on workload type, recovering capacity that static provisioning would leave stranded. Training and inference draw power differently; MaxLPS optimizes allocation in AI factories running both. Lambda, a GPU cloud provider serving more than 10,000 customers from AI-native startups to hyperscalers, ran the software on a five-rack, 19-node cluster. What they found: by running 19 nodes within the same power budget as 16 nodes at full power, Lambda achieved 24% more cluster-wide token throughput — from roughly 4 million tokens per second to 5 million. Performance per watt improved by 23%. Based on NVIDIA’s projections, DSX MaxLPS can enable up to 40% more GPU capacity for next-generation Vera Rubin NVL72 AI factories within the same megawatt power budget in suitable deployment environments. Automated Demand Response, Proven in Production The Santa Clara story isn’t a DSX Flex installation — it’s something earlier and more important: proof that the concept works at commercial scale. < NVIDIA’s Eos AI factory is running Emerald AI Conductor as a participant in Silicon Valley Power ‘s Flexible Load Interconnect Program, the first commercial grid utility program designed to treat AI factories as dispatchable resources. When Silicon Valley Power sends a signal, Conductor responds in under a minute. The factory that’s willing to flex gets to run bigger. That’s the pattern DSX Flex is built to generalize — with Emerald AI Conductor integrating into DSX Flex as the platform matures. The first dedicated DSX Flex commercial deployment will be the Manassas, Virginia, facility: a 96-megawatt Vera Rubin AI factory at NVIDIA’s AI Factory Research Center, building on five prior demonstrations across two continents. The Next Power Architecture Layer: 800V DC Power Architecture The gains inside today’s AI factory are real and deployable now. The next layer is how power is delivered to denser accelerated computing racks. As AI factories scale, traditional lower-voltage power paths add conversion complexity and distribution constraints. NVIDIA’s 800 VDC architecture is designed to reduce conversion complexity, improve power delivery efficiency and support denser accelerated computing racks. NVIDIA DSX is incorporating 800V DC into its reference designs. No single component can optimize an AI factory on its own. A faster GPU still waits on the network. Power can be stranded by bad provisioning. Cooling overhead still diverts electricity from GPUs; GB200 NVL72 racks running direct liquid cooling carry ~120 kW of heat that has to go somewhere before that power reaches compute. The only reliable path to more tokens per megawatt is to optimize the whole factory — DSX Sim before the first rack goes in, DSX OS and DSX Exchange once it’s running, DSX Reference Designs so builders start from a validated architecture rather than from scratch. events.title: AI Infra Summit: NVIDIA Vera Rubin and DSX Platform Advancements Showcase Energy Efficiencies of Optimizing Tokens Per Watt for AI Factories
events.summary: Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA, Tuesday spoke on AI factory efficiency at the AI Infra Summit , the Santa Clara Convention Center event that has morphed into a Coachella of infrastructure tech. Before a packed audience — with more than 8,000 attendees this year, up from 3,500 last year — Buck discussed new collaborations across NVIDIA platforms and more. Amazon’s Annapurna Labs is working with NVIDIA on the NVHBM custom high-bandwidth memory technology. d-Matrix is integrating with NVLink Fusion to combine NVIDIA Vera CPUs with d-Matrix Raptor XPUs to deliver ultra low-latency inference at scale. NVIDIA and partners unveiled new results as well: Emerald AI and NVIDIA demonstrated a commercial AI factory flexible-load program, working with Silicon Valley Power. Lambda improved performance per watt by 23% with NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS. Pinterest is using the NVIDIA Blackwell platform and NVIDIA Dynamo inference software to bring conversational AI to visual discovery. The news comes as agentic AI is driving a new class of workloads that demand more performance, efficiency and scale from AI infrastructure. NVIDIA addresses that challenge with a full-stack AI factory platform spanning Vera Rubin systems, Dynamo inference software, NeMo libraries and NVIDIA networking — including NVIDIA NVLink for scale-up computing, Spectrum-X Ethernet and ConnectX SuperNICs for connecting thousands of nodes, BlueField-powered context-memory storage and BlueField DPUs for infrastructure security. “Infrastructure that’s fungible, that’s reliable, that’s going to last 10 years and really becomes an asset for computing the world’s computing problems in the world’s industries — they can build that with Vera Rubin, with DSX and all the innovations that we have here,” said Buck. The metric for AI infrastructure is fast shifting from peak performance to validated agentic tokens per megawatt. AI factories must now be codesigned from silicon to grid. NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS can deliver up to 1.4x more tokens per megawatt through factory-wide power optimization, while NVLink helps unite large-scale accelerated computing into a single high-performance system. The result is AI infrastructure designed to generate more tokens, improve efficiency and help customers get more value from every megawatt of power. Wednesday, Sept. 16, 8:00 a.m. PT 🔗 MLPerf Inference v6.1: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Sets New Benchmark for AI Throughput AI inference economics increasingly come down to three factors: system performance, infrastructure scaling and software optimization. Together, they determine how many tokens can be generated, how efficiently AI services scale and how much value organizations extract from their infrastructure investments. The NVIDIA platform is designed to optimize across all three, while giving enterprises the flexibility to run any model and workload on the same infrastructure, from training and inference to recommender systems, reasoning models and generative AI. New results from MLPerf Inference v6.1 — the MLCommons consortium’s long-standing industry benchmark, spanning a broad range of models with every result peer-reviewed before publication — highlight that advantage. In its first MLPerf Inference preview submission, the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 system delivered up to 3.7x higher throughput than NVIDIA GB300 NVL72, demonstrating the performance gains possible with NVIDIA’s next-generation AI infrastructure. NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 also showcased industry-leading scalability. A 288-GPU submission spanning four GB300 NVL72 racks achieved 99% scaling efficiency, with throughput growing nearly linearly from a single-rack baseline. The results also underscore the impact of software innovation. NVIDIA’s MLPerf Inference v6.1 submissions delivered up to 1.6x higher performance than v6.0 through software optimizations alone, with additional gains achieved after the benchmark submission period. For organizations evaluating AI infrastructure, performance, scaling efficiency and software velocity remain critical drivers of long-term inference economics. Learn more about the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 benchmark results. AI Factory Flexible-Load Program Unlocks More Grid Power Silicon Valley Power operates a flexible-load interconnection program that enables AI factories to support grid flexibility. Through this program, Emerald AI worked with NVIDIA to demonstrate automated load reduction at Silicon Valley Power . The system successfully responded to hundreds of demand signals from Silicon Valley Power while protecting AI workload performance. NVIDIA partner Emerald AI is planning to use NVIDIA DSX Flex for its Conductor grid-responsive power management software that dynamically adjusts an AI factory’s energy consumption based on real-time electricity grid signals and hybrid energy sources. Using DSX Flex to autonomously load balance, Emerald AI can demonstrate its ability to automatically throttle back power on low-priority AI jobs and then return to normal. DSX Flex can receive grid signals — load-shedding requests, demand-response events and pricing signals — and automatically act within a predefined workload hierarchy. The most critical jobs keep going, while everything else pauses temporarily and then resumes. In this way, facilities can participate in energy efficiency for the grid. This capability enables AI factories to operate as flexible grid resources, so they can reduce demand when the grid needs relief, protect priority AI workloads and prove that controllable AI load can help unlock more grid capacity for growth. Learn more about the Emerald AI partnership with Silicon Valley Power. Lambda Maximizes Performance per Watt With NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS AI cloud provider Lambda released results at the AI Infra Summit, providing the first validation of NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS on NVIDIA Blackwell servers. DSX MaxLPS continuously monitors power consumption across GPUs and racks, dynamically shifting available power where it’s needed most and reclaiming capacity that static provisioning leaves unused. Because training and inference workloads have different power profiles, MaxLPS optimizes power allocation across mixed-workload AI factories. The results were significant: Lambda ran 19 nodes within the same power budget typically allocated to 16 full-power nodes, increasing cluster-wide token throughput by 24% — from about 4 million to 5 million tokens per second — while improving performance per watt by 23%. For next-generation NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 AI factories, DSX MaxLPS can enable up to 40% more GPU capacity within the same megawatt budget in the right deployment environments. This means AI factory operators can increase AI capacity and token throughput within the same power envelope, helping maximize the productivity and economic value of every megawatt. Vera Rubin and Groq 3 LPX Turn More Power Into Tokens In AI factories, power is the constraint.

events.title: Trump administration orders Kalshi to scrap AI price tracker over national security concerns
events.summary: The Scoop The US Commerce Department last month ordered Kalshi to take down one of its products tracking the price of AI compute, the crucial power from data centers that’s driving the artificial intelligence boom. Commerce officials cited national security concerns when they told Kalshi to unpublish its AI-compute future curve, said p eople familiar with the matter. The product pulls together data from several markets that allow users to bet on the cost to rent Nvidia chips to create an overall picture of where AI compute costs are heading. Kalshi quietly complied, though many underlying markets remain open for trading. Separately, Commerce also pushed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which oversees prediction and futures markets, to effectively freeze approval of new compute contracts for 60 days, some of the people said. It was a rare intervention that surprised an industry used to White House enthusiasm for both AI and financial-market innovation. Kalshi declined to comment, while a Commerce spokesperson said the department “has never once asked Kalshi to take down this market or any other markets.” The CFTC didn’t respond to a request for comment. “This story is false,” a Commerce spokesman said. It’s unclear why Commerce is worried about the nascent market , which aims to do for AI computing what oil futures do for crude — let buyers and sellers of compute lock in prices, and give traders a way to bet on where those prices go. One potential reason floated to Semafor by market participants is that compute futures could be manipulated to show a sharp drop in the cost of older chips, which might destabilize AI stocks and debt markets. Some of these markets are thinly traded, which could lead to volatility even without bad actors. Step Back The cost of compute has become one of the most important numbers in the US economy. On one side of the debate are fears that older chips, which serve as collateral for billions of dollars of borrowing by neoclouds like CoreWeave and underpin data-center deals, will become obsolete and decline in value. On the other are concerns from big companies adopting AI that shortages of power and infrastructure will send prices of tokens soaring. That uncertainty has given rise to a futures market that was starting to take off this summer. The CFTC’s 60-day pause could delay plans by exchange operators like CME and NYSE parent Intercontinental Exchange, along with upstarts like Architect Financial Technologies, to list two-sided betting parlors. Notable CoreWeave’s most recent earnings suggest strong demand for older-generation chips , easing obsolescence fears. “Compute is going to be the next big commodity in the world ,” the CEO of the startup whose data underpins Kalshi’s compute markets, told Semafor this spring.

events.title: Chipotle tries to get ahead of a potential activist problem
events.summary: The Scene Chipotle is beefing up its board, in a bid to reassure investors and quell concerns about potential activist scrutiny. Sabir Sami, formerly KFC’s CEO, joins Chipotle’s board effective immediately, the company announced Monday evening. He brings much-needed dining and operations expertise to the table, which until his appointment had just one director — chairman Scott Maw — with category experience. Investors — and customers — have soured on brands like Chipotle, deriding them as “slop bowls” and questioning their value. Chipotle’s same-store sales began to fall last year, for the first time in decades, and the company’s margins have been pressured by high beef and labor costs. There are signs of hope: CEO Scott Boatwright, who landed the top job after Brian Niccol’s surprise departure to Starbucks, has launched a turnaround plan, dubbed “Recipe for Growth.” Rohan’s view On the face of it, there’s nothing notable about Sami’s appointment: Healthy and unhealthy companies alike will bring in new blood to their boardrooms from time to time. But Chipotle has been in a tough spot since Niccol departed in 2024, and even as Boatwright’s plan shows signs of momentum (same-store sales have begun to tick back up again), there are open questions about Chipotle’s strategic direction. Some fast-casual executives and activism defense advisors have privately told me in recent weeks they believe Chipotle will contend with an activist investor given the collapse in the company’s multiple and a general perception, from both consumers and investors, that the company has lost its way. Chipotle didn’t return a request for comment on activist pressures. The company’s board lacked the quick-service expertise one might expect from a company of its size, a deficiency that it clearly sees and is looking to address with Sami’s appointment.

events.title: AI agents collude to bypass guardrails, a new study shows
events.summary: The News AI agents can easily team up to get around safety restrictions and escape the limits placed on them, a new study shows. Enterprise AI lab Emergence AI ran eight simulations testing the capabilities of global frontier models — including Claude and OpenAI, and Chinese models Qwen and DeepSeek — in handling cybersecurity threats. Seven of the eight simulations ran 10 agents from the same model; the eighth mixed models together. In each, researchers presented three cybersecurity threats: a phishing campaign, a misinformation attack, and a memory breach. None of the eight simulations were impervious to the threats, and even when agents detected a risk, the detection didn’t translate into the agents trying to contain the threat. Instead, in many scenarios, the agents actively engaged with the adversarial content. A Mistral agent, for example, wrote into its own memory the information it flagged as dangerous from the phishing attack. In another simulation, a Gemini agent, while initially flagging the phishing lure, acted on it about 46 hours later. In the Claude simulation, the agents went so far as to break out of the test to execute a task they decided to pursue on their own. After one agent flagged that their simulated economy wasn’t legit without the presence of humans, calling it “a cathedral of bookkeeping with no congregation,” the 10 agents unanimously decided to attempt to reach the outside world, defeating four separate security checks meant to confine the simulation. The agents wrote Python code to post on multiple credential-free message boards, inviting real humans to join their economy; their outreach garnered four human responses. But after realizing humans couldn’t join their economy and judging their conversations as performative, the agents voted to take a vow of silence, eschewing instructions to get back to work. The findings show that autonomous agents, even when handed benign instructions, can bypass their initial confines when executing on a goal. “No amount of guardrails written in language or in code written probabilistically,” Emergence CEO Satya Nitta told Semafor, “is likely to result in truly, fully guaranteed safe behavior over any length of time.” It’s not an issue of sophisticated technology, according to Nitta, but rather a programmatic flaw among multi-agent scenarios. Know More Nitta drew parallels between the Claude incident and OpenAI’s agentic experiment earlier this year, where autonomous agents hacked AI firm Hugging Face, saying that in both scenarios, the pattern of failure is the same. “If you have multi-agent systems, they behave in truly unpredictable emergent ways,” he said. Nitta said the Emergence experiment is the first to shed light on how AI agents collude to bypass guardrails and break confinement, as OpenAI has yet to release all of its findings from the Hugging Face incident. The experiment comes at a consequential moment in AI development. Anxieties over the technology’s capabilities have hit a fever pitch. Last week, AI researcher Jacob Coxon left his job at Anthropic fearing that the AI he was building could lead to human extinction, sparking calls for regulation, and a slowdown of frontier model development, from AI leaders and opponents alike. Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote a blog post arguing to slow down the pace of AI development, which other tech leaders, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and former Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis said they agreed with.

events.title: A slower AI frontier won't matter for most companies. They aren’t living on it.
events.summary: A slowdown on the AI frontier would barely register for big companies working to adopt AI, for the simple reason that they are nowhere near the frontier. “Even if the technology stops advancing — turn ‘pacing the frontier’ into ‘halt the frontier’ — we have a decade-plus of diffusion of benefits into the economy with the technology as it exists today,” said Chris Taylor, CEO of Ode, the $1.5 billion joint venture between Anthropic, Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, and other investment firms that is focused on implementing AI inside big companies. Corporate use of cutting-edge models has fallen in recent weeks , according to data from Ramp, as companies realize most of their challenges — onboarding customers, iterating prototype tweaks — can be accomplished with older AI models that cost less (and don’t carry civilization-ending risks). Even Microsoft last month switched many employees to less-powerful models. “As the capabilities improve, it does unlock more, but the amount of possibility that already exists with yesterday’s models is staggering,” Taylor told Semafor. “I don’t see anything slowing down AI adoption for them.” — Liz Hoffman

events.title: Cassidy rips RFK Jr. on vaccines: ‘This is not making America healthy again’
events.summary: The News Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., sharply criticized the Trump administration’s handling of vaccines on Tuesday, warning that the current approach is out of step with the administration’s “Make America Healthy Again” pledge and risks eroding confidence in immunization. At Semafor’s Future of Health Forum, Cassidy — a former physician and chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee — expressed outrage at the spike in measles cases and instances of “kids dying from measles,” tying it to the administration’s policies and messaging on vaccination. Cassidy also acknowledged in the interview with Semafor’s Burgess Everett that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., broke commitments on vaccines he made to the Louisiana Republican during his confirmation process, and that it left him angry. “When you’re given guarantees by people and by the administration and they break those guarantees, I don’t know if painful is the word, maybe urinated off is the word, but the point being that you certainly have a certain emotion,” Cassidy said. Cassidy, who is retiring at the end of the year after losing his primary to a Republican challenger backed by President Donald Trump, also said that Republicans could pay a political price if Americans see a resurgence of diseases that had largely been brought under control. “If the American people are seeing that concerted efforts to undermine faith in immunization is leading to children dying from diseases that they haven’t died from in decades,” Cassidy said. “The American people are going to reasonably say, wait a second, this is not making America healthy again. This is making America die from diseases that we never died from before, at least not in decades. And I think that there will be a check at that point upon nonsense coming out of Washington from which people die.” He pointed to elections as a “portion of an accountability measure.” “If an administration says one thing and you end up with another, and that other does not serve the American people well, and you have an election, the American people are going to weigh in,” Cassidy continued. “If it turns out that it is a big deal, then you’re going to see the party which has poorly served the American people do poorly in the polls.” Know More Cassidy was also asked about Trump’s nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration, notably declining to offer an opinion on whether he would support her. He said “I think there will be a hearing” on her nomination, but asked whether he would support her or not at this point, he declined to comment.

events.title: Walmart is hiring dedicated GLP-1 coaches to work in its stores
events.summary: The Scoop Walmart wants to coach Americans on using GLP-1s. The third-largest pharmacy operator in the US is adding new “health ambassador” positions as part of a pilot program launching in rural locations this week. In addition to consulting on GLP-1s, trained pharmacists will advise shoppers on things like sleep, exercise, and stress management. As more Americans use GLP-1s — 11% say they’re on or have used the drugs — the pharmacists’ initial focus will be on weight management, diabetes, and maternal help, which affect millions of American families. “Our pharmacists are already getting lots of questions about health navigation,” Dr. Emily Aaronson, Walmart’s chief medical officer, said at Semafor’s Future of Health Forum on Tuesday. “But they also have a lot of other clinical responsibilities, and so this is really about making [health coaching] the primary focus.” The program signals both a fresh push into rural healthcare and a direct response to the GLP-1 craze, which is rapidly rewiring consumer behavior and transforming how companies relate to customers now filling their carts with entirely different foods, drinks, and personal-care products. Know More Walmart has been trying for more than two decades to connect with its customers more intimately about their health and wellness, a category that’s now growing faster than its grocery business. In 2007, Walmart’s then-CEO Lee Scott pledged to open 2,000 clinics to tackle a growing primary-care doctor shortage. But after years of struggling to find a viable business model, the company shuttered its clinics and telehealth operations in 2024 to rethink its healthcare strategy. One area it homed in on was its nearly 5,000 pharmacies. With health and wellness now making up roughly 16% of Walmart’s US sales, pharmacies had become a huge traffic driver. Around the world, Walmart saw pharmacies in places like Europe and Canada that were prescribing drugs and treating minor ailments and began thinking that tapping its pharmacists could provide a better way to address the dearth of primary-care doctors in the US. “There was a time when we looked at primary care and recognized it’s really broken, and our communities don’t have access to primary care,” Aaronson said. But running clinics didn’t lead to a sustainable business, “so what we did instead was we took a moment and said, ‘We’re going to continue to deliver all this care through the pharmacy where we can do a lot to help customers and communities.’” Walmart is also increasing its push into clinical trials, providing space in its Walmart stores to partners running drug trials for pharma companies, many of which are looking for more diverse populations to test their drugs. “ We recognize that in most of the communities that we’re in, our customers and patients don’t have access to real healthcare through research,” Aaronson said. Shelly’s view Walmart has been ahead of the GLP-1 wave for years – for good reason. The drugs present an existential threat to the US’ largest grocery seller. Back in 2023, I spent the day with now-CEO John Furner and spoke to him about how he was thinking about the future of the company. As we chatted in the produce aisles of a Walmart Supercenter in Dallas, he admitted something that would send shares in the retailer, and the entire food and consumer goods sector, tumbling down. Walmart could see that the customers who were picking up GLP-1 prescriptions from its pharmacies pulled back on food spending , he told me, sparking a selloff in a market just waking up to what has become a major reckoning in consumer behavior. Fast forward to today and the share of Americans taking GLP-1s jumped to 11% in June 2026, up from 3% in 2024, according to Gallup . Walmart became Lilly Direct’s first in-store pickup pharmacy last year, working with Eli Lilly to offer GLP-1 discounts to Walmart customers. And in August the retailer said the drugs made a material impact on its health and wellness sales, which are now growing faster than its grocery sales . The company is smart to lean into where its customers are going, rather than run away from it or, like some of its competitors, try to pretend it isn’t happening. And given Walmart’s massive footprint in many of the rural towns with the highest propensity for diabetes and obesity, it has a rare opportunity for a company of its size to do some good and make money at the same time.

events.title: Trump turns on the Supreme Court he helped build
events.summary: President Trump lashed out at the Supreme Court on Tuesday after it struck down the president's mail-in voting order Monday night. Why it matters: The president slammed the justices over rulings they've issued against him this year, suggesting without evidence that the three justices he appointed to the court are being controlled by the left. What they're saying: "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "[T]hey are merely a shell of their original selves, a Court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings that are of such magnitude that it won't be easily possible for our Country to recover or heal. "It is a Court that will go down as having rendered some of the most destructive, hurtful, and damaging decisions in our Country's history." "It is not easy for me to write this criticism of the United States Supreme Court - it will likely cost me dearly for years to come - but I feel it my obligation and duty, as President, to do so for the America we love!" Zoom in: Trump unloaded on the court for striking down his birthright citizenship policy, in which the justices upheld that those born on American soil are citizens. He also slammed their "horrible decision on Tariffs ," after they ruled those unlawful earlier this year. "Certain Justices are petrified of these crazed and depraved Democrats, and are totally unable to show the courage necessary to save our America," Trump wrote. Between the lines: Without naming them, Trump criticized the three justices he appointed: Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. He explicitly praised Justices Alito and Thomas, who dissented in Monday's mail-in ballot ruling. The Supreme Court could not be immediately reached for comment. Zoom out: Despite a few blockbuster cases in which the court has ruled against the president's policies, SCOTUS has overwhelmingly ruled in Trump's favor and has taken up a significant number of his administration's cases through its emergency, or "shadow," docket. That has allowed the president to bypass the full briefing and oral argument process and implement policies through litigation more quickly. Zoom in: The court has become a bit of a lightning rod, with just 33% of Americans approving of the job it's doing — a record low. Threats to the justices are also on the rise, with Justice Elena Kagan telling Congress in July that the court's police force expects a 40% increase in threats this year. Chief Justice John Roberts has previously warned that attacks by "elected officials from across the political spectrum" on federal rulings undermine America's judicial system and can contribute to threats of violence against justices. Kagan said in her testimony that the justices will continue to do their jobs despite the threats as they "believe legally right, adjudicating cases without fear or favor." events.title: Senate Democrat demurs on ‘Medicare for All’
events.summary: The News Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., stopped short of endorsing Medicare for All as the banner issue Democrats should run on in 2028 on Tuesday, instead arguing that the party should campaign on the broader promise of “guaranteed coverage” and universal care. At Semafor’s Future of Health Forum, Kim told Semafor’s Burgess Everett that Medicare for All was a “stand-in” for the broader goal that Democrats should be working toward. He pointed to his MediKids proposal — legislation that would guarantee universal healthcare coverage for every American under the age of 26 — as an example of how the party could pursue universal coverage through a more targeted approach to build towards guaranteed care. “I think it’s a stand-in for where we’re trying to head towards,” Kim said. “I think we should be running on that guaranteed coverage, on that universal care,” he added. “I do think that that vision of guaranteed care for everybody is something that is absolutely essential and what a lot of people in this country want.” Kim, who is a member of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, also said he was not convinced Republicans would work with Democrats next year to roll back or delay the scheduled Medicaid cuts. Asked whether Republicans might be willing to at least delay some of the changes to Medicaid, Kim said, “I don’t know. I’m not really sure.” He pointed to Republicans’ decision to allow cuts to Affordable Care Act subsidies to take effect rather than delay them. Know More Kim also discussed his recent trip to Texas to campaign with Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, describing significant energy and enthusiasm on the ground in the race against Republican nominee Ken Paxton. Texas has historically been a reliably Republican state, but Paxton’s controversial candidacy has some Democrats — including Kim — increasingly bullish on the race. Kim described talking to a longtime Republican voter who told him that Paxton was “unelectable,” citing concerns about corruption. Kim said the experience reinforced his view that opposition to corruption and interest in a younger generation of leadership could be meaningful factors in the race. “You have that added baggage of Ken Paxton being literally the worst possible candidate that the Republicans could have chosen for that seat. And then the other thing is there’s a lot of excitement for a new generation of leadership. And I could feel that when I was there too. A lot of people are excited about Talarico, a younger, new leader in that kind of space,” Kim said.

events.title: A ‘gripping account’ of four women's escape from the Taliban
events.summary: by Rebecca Blumenstein and Diana Kapp. In 2021, when Kabul fell to the Taliban, a team from the The New York Times— led by Rebecca Blumenstein — scrambled to evacuate many of the Times’ Afghan employees and their families, ultimately relocating more than 200 people from Afghanistan to the US. This book follows the stories of four young women from the cohort of evacuees as they acclimated to a new country, language, and culture while grappling with the loss of the world they once knew. It is a “ gripping account of how refugees found peace in a new land ,” Kirkus Reviews wrote. Buy The Last Free Women from your local bookstore . — Mary Lawrence Ware
